utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-04-78-PT, the Prosecutor versus Rahim Ademi and Mirko Norac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. May I have the appearances. Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Kenneth Scott for the Office of the Prosecutor, and with me this morning are Ann Sutherland and Laurie Sartorio, and our case manager Lakshmie Walpita.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am counsel for General Ademi, attorney Cedo Prodanovic, and with me is my colleague, Ms. Jadranka Slokovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prodanovic. And for Mr. Norac.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Zeljko Olujic appearing for Mirko Norac. I am an attorney from Zagreb in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olujic. Then we have some guests, representatives of the Republic of Croatia. Could they please introduce themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I am representative of the state of Croatia. I am the president of the Croatian Academy of Science and the counsellor of the Ministry of Justice. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your name is Mr. Horvatic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: My name is Zeljko Horvatic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Horvatic. And you're accompanied by -- good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MULJACIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. I am Jaksa Muljacic, I am co-representative of the Republic of Croatia here. I am Assistant Minister of justice. And Sinisa Milevoj on behalf of the Embassy of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning to you, Mr. Horvatic, Mr. Muljacic, and Mr. Milevoj. And then amicus curiae that appears today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I am Professor Davor Krapac, University of Zagreb School of Law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krapac. And I do understand that Professor Damaska was not able to come today, but you have come and submitted together an amicus curiae brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We're in this courtroom today to hear further submissions and to hear further argument in relation to a motion filed by the Prosecution to refer the cases against Mr. Norac and Mr. Ademi to be further tried in a Croatian court. Before we further proceed, I'd like to ask the Defence, since the accused are not present, whether the accused agreed that we would proceed in their absence. We all know that Mr. Ademi is on provisional release. Mr. Norac is at this moment detained in Croatia. Could you please express yourself on the absence of the accused and whether they agree that we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while General Ademi was the only accused in this case about a year and a half ago, he had an opportunity to declare himself about the anticipated referral of this case to the Republic of Croatia and he agrees with the motion. And also he agrees that the case be referred to the Croatian judiciary. He has expressed no wish to be present at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as you know, Mr. Mirko Norac, my client, has been sentenced to 12 years in prison and he is serving his sentence in the proper institution. This is the reason why, by your leave, I was able to extend the deadline for my response to the Chamber. I consulted my client and he agrees without any reservations that today's session be held without his presence. He agrees that he not be present today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then proceed in the absence of the accused. This is the first time that this Tribunal hears a motion in a public hearing on a referral of cases, and a lot of basic issues arise. The parties have submitted extensive written submissions already. I'd like to invite the parties, and that will take us approximately into the first break -- I'd like to invite the parties to briefly summarise their positions as taken until now because it is the first time that a matter is dealt with in a public hearing. So a brief summary of its position taken until now and any additional issues to be raised since you now are aware of what the other parties, what amici and what the Croatian government has submitted to this court. I would first like to give the opportunity to the Prosecution. I expect the Prosecution to do that in 20 to 25 minutes. Then I'll give an opportunity to counsel for Mr. Ademi and then for counsel for Mr. Norac. Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Counsel, representatives of the Republic of Croatia, and amici curiae. This is a hard situation. For many of us, sending any serious war crimes case away to be prosecuted anywhere else goes against the grain. We want to finish the job and we want to finish the job here. Let there be no mistake: Given adequate time and resources, the prosecutor, Madam Del Ponte would prefer to prosecute this case here; I would prefer to prosecute this case here. I would prefer to prosecute these two accused concerning the horrible crimes that are alleged against them if there was adequate time and resources to do so. But at the same time, all of us, the Tribunal, all of us here are in a situation that has existed from the very beginning, from the first day that this Tribunal opened its doors and still exists today. It was always known and is known today that this Tribunal would never and will never be able to prosecute all of the serious war crimes and all of the terrible perpetrators from the horrible Balkan wars. What I said a moment ago, I submit, summarises the situation we are in: We want to finish the job and we want to finish the job here. Therein lies the dilemma. We want to finish the job here, but in order to do that and to still finish the bigger job, some cases, even quite important ones - and, I would add, are there any that are not important? - But even quite important ones must be prosecuted and decided somewhere else. That is the reality. Having said this, the Prosecutor affirms and, Your Honours, I affirm this morning that there can be no transfer that results or would result in impunity. At the end of the day if this Bench, this Referral Bench, decides that this case or any case cannot be transferred without an unreasonable risk to the cause of justice, then the case should stay here. In going forward I note the directions given by the Security Council to this institution. In paragraph 4 of the Security Counsel Resolution 1534, the Security Council stated: "It calls on the ICTY and the prosecutors here to review the case-load of the ICTY, in particular with a view to determining which cases should be proceeded with and which should be transferred to competent national jurisdictions as well as the measures that need to be taken to meet the completion strategies referred to Resolution 1503." In that reference to Resolution 1503 in 2003, the Security Council stated: "Recalling and re-affirming in the strongest terms the statement of 23rd July, 2002, made by the President of the Security Council which endorsed the ICTY strategy for completing investigations by the end of 2004, all trial activities of first instance by the end of 2008, and all of its work in 2010 by concentrating on the prosecution and trial of the most senior leaders suspected of being most responsible for crimes within the ICTY jurisdiction and transferring cases involving those who may not" -- who may not -- "bear this level of responsibility to competent jurisdictions as appropriate, as well as the strengthening of the capacity of such jurisdictions. Both the President and the Prosecutor of this Tribunal have made similar statements and commitments. As the President His Honour Judge Meron stated at the Security Council on 29 June of last year: "As the Council recognised in Resolutions 1503 and 1534, the ability to refer cases of intermediate- and lower-rank accused to domestic jurisdictions including the planned war-crimes chamber within the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina is an essential prerequisite to the fulfilment of the completion strategy." President Meron also reported the statement by the OSCE Mission to Croatia that "There is no reason to believe" -- and I know there's been some questions that have been raised that will be discussed probably in the course of the day, but President Meron stated in June of last year: "There is no reason to believe that the Croatian judiciary would not be able to handle a limited number of cases in a fair and efficient way, particularly if assigned to those judges and prosecutors who have already received special training and resources." President Meron made similar statements, more recently on September 23 of 2004, again emphasising the importance of transfer of cases as part of the completion strategy of this Tribunal. I will not read his comments at length in the interest of time. However, President Meron recognised also the importance that "In using the 11 bis process to integrate Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia and Serbia and Montenegro into the process of bringing offenders to justice, that itself will have benefits that go well beyond a reduction of the Tribunal's case-load and promoting the completion strategy. Involving these national governments in the process will bring reconciliation and justice to the region as well as promote the development of commitment to the rule of law. "National courts can only play this role, however, if trials are not used for political purposes and if they meet the standards of due process and fair trial." Referring to the judiciary particularly in Zagreb, President Meron stated: "I am optimistic about their growing capability to try war-crime cases according to international human-rights and due-process standards. I have been advised by the OSCE Mission to Croatia in a letter dated 12 November 2004 that a limited number of transferred cases could likely be dealt with adequately by a limited number of courts in Croatia." The Prosecutor too, Madam Del Ponte, addressing the Security Council and in various public statements has echoed these same remarks and stressed the importance of the transfer of cases to the Tribunal's completion strategy. She also recognises that beyond the assistance given to the Tribunal in completing its own work, the successful prosecution of war-crimes cases in the countries of the former Yugoslavia is an important milestone in marking the reconciliation and progress being made in these areas. Having said this, and as I said a moment ago, the Office of the Prosecutor fully understands the importance of ensuring that the transfer of cases is properly done with full consideration of the various factors and questions that may be involved in these decisions. In turning to this case, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Norac/Ademi case, we observe at the outset as we have observed before in our very first, earliest submissions that this is a case that could go either way. While some of the Rule 11 bis candidate cases might be considered to more clearly involve lower-level accused or less serious charges - if we can use that terminology given the cases and types of crimes that this Tribunal deals, if any are less serious - the level of the accused here and the seriousness of the offences here would make this case fully suitable to remain at the ICTY for prosecution. In this sense, it may be thought by some that this is not the best case to first reach this point in the process. To some extent, I suppose, that was the luck of the draw. Some other cases might possibly have reached a Referral Bench before this one. But inevitably, and in any event, the cases that the Chambers and the Tribunal will consider, that the Referral Bench will consider, will cover a range of accused and a range of situations. And on balance the Prosecutor believed that this is a case -- believes and believed then at the time of her initial submission -- that this is a case that while fully suitable as an ICTY case is also a case that can properly be transferred or considered for transfer by the judges assigned to this determination. Rule 11 bis states: "In determining whether to refer the case, the Trial Chamber shall, in accordance with United Nations Security Council Resolution 1534, consider the gravity of the crimes charged and the level of responsibility of the accused..." Once again, most of us involved in this process find it difficult and somewhat artificial to assign rankings to cases involving some of the world's most horrible crimes. The killing or abuse of 10 persons or 50 persons or 100 persons, let alone thousands, is not to be condoned or minimised in any way. And yet the Security Council resolution and completion strategy requires us to in fact engage in such a process, at least to some extent. We also think it important to observe the following before turning to some of the more specific questions about the case. And I realise my comments now will only be essentially introductory to many topics and issues that I am sure will be discussed in the course of the day. We think it's important to note at the outset, Mr. President, Your Honours, this motion, the motion before the Bench, has only limited connection to the assessment of the overall condition of the Croatian legal and judicial system as a whole. We are aware, of course, of various reports and studies and assessments that have been made, including such as those by OSCE. With respect, however, the matter before the Bench concerns this one case and the referral of this one case to one of the best courts in Croatia, one of the specialised courts that have been designed to handle war-crimes cases; with the assignment, we are promised, we have been promised, of the best prosecutors; where, at least as to procedural matters and practices, the most recent reformed laws will apply, which include receiving and admitting ICTY evidence. The Chamber, respectfully, need not consider in our view what might happen in some other Croatian court in Split or Vukovar or in some other outlying area or another war-crime case in some other conditions or circumstances. It is the referral of this case under the conditions and commitments that have been made by the Government of Croatia. Further, it goes without saying and is not saying anything secret: Croatia knows and will know that this case will be watched with great scrutiny from beginning to end, and if the ICTY is not satisfied with the case, is not satisfied with the Croatian proceedings, the ICTY will order -- at least the Office of the Prosecutor will seek that the referral be withdrawn and the case be returned here. I turn briefly to the two topics of the gravity of the offences charged and the level of the accused. And again, for purposes of time, let me just say as to the gravity of the offences charged we've outlined those in several of our submissions, particularly the submission that was made in November. These are indeed serious crimes. What happened in the Medak Pocket in September 1993 was truly horrendous. While it involved a relatively small area, approximately only 5 kilometres by 5 kilometres in size, it involved essentially the total disruption of the Serb areas, houses, residences, villages in that area; in our submission done intentionally, done systematically, resulting in the deaths of many people, at least 29 -- a conservative number, at least 29 Serb civilians, many of the victims be women and elderly, shot at close range, shot in the back. The majority of the buildings in the entire Medak Pocket, more than 164 homes, 148 barns and outbuildings, were intentionally destroyed by fire or explosives. The investigation showed that unfortunately most of these crimes, these alleged crimes occurred, after a cease-fire was in effect; that is, they did not happen during combat operations but after the fighting was over. Oil was intentionally poured and dead animals thrown into wells in order to pollute them. The investigation further showed that all or most of these alleged crimes occurred while the Croatian army forces were deliberately preventing the UN peacekeeping forces, UNPROFOR, from entering the area. As a result of this widespread and systematic campaign, the Medak Pocket was rendered unlivable. It's the Prosecutor's view and the basis of the indictment that that was what was intended: to drive the Serbs from this pocket, from this area, and make conditions so uninhabitable that they would not return. It is indeed a serious case. In terms of the level of responsibility of the accused, we submit to Your Honours, and we again address this in our submissions, that both Mr. Ademi and Mr. Norac fall in the upper -- fall in the middle, approximately the middle- to upper-half of the various accused that have been processed, indicted, processed, adjudicated at this Tribunal. I don't think in any stretch of the imagination and with honesty they can be considered lower-level figures. Mr. Ademi was a senior official, a senior officer and very high in the chain of command. He was the deputy commander and then appointed acting commander of the Gospic military district, the position he held at the time of the charged offences. Mr. Norac was a commander of the HV 6th Guards Brigade which became the 9th Guards Motorised Brigade which was the principal motorised unit involved in these alleged atrocities. We submitted to the Chamber before a chart, Annex 1, that was part of our November submission, which indicated on the one side the approximate level of the accused in relation to the chain of command in the Croatian military starting with President Tudjman, of course, at the top as commander-in-chief, and continuing down to the private soldier, if you will. On the other side of that chart we provided a comparison, if you will, of other ICTY cases and other 11 bis candidate cases. In general and by summary, the level of the accused Ademi can be directly compared among others to the ICTY accused Krstic, Tihomir Blaskic, and Stanislav Galic. We believe that Mr. Ademi was at at least a comparable level to those. As to Mr. Norac, he can be compared to such ICTY accused as Mario Cerkez, Vidoje Blagojevic and Mladen Naletilic, "Tuta." And indeed, and for better or worse, the chart would show that many, many people have been prosecuted by this Tribunal, rightly or wrongly, at substantially lower levels than both Mr. Ademi and Mr. Norac. I think that I'm probably perhaps reaching the limits of my time at the moment. Let me just preview a couple of comments, a couple of the other issues that will be discussed in the course of the day. One, of course, important question the Chamber has raised which substantive law would be applicable to the case that is transferred to Croatia. It appears to us -- all the parties, and the Republic of Croatia and the amici agree, appear to agree with perhaps some variation of certainty, perhaps with some qualification, but generally that in fact 1993 law, the law in effect at the time of the crimes, would apply. There may be some qualification to this if the -- if the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights, Article 7(2) would be applied which does provide for or allows as an exception to the general prohibition against the retroactive criminal law: "The trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which at the time when it was committed was criminal according to the general principles of law recognised by civilised nations." And we would submit, Your Honours, that the nature of the crimes here and the theories of responsibility were matters of existing international law at the time this conduct occurred in 1993. Again, only briefly now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, before you move on, you may have noticed especially in the respect of the direct applicability of norms of international law, be it treaty law or be it customary law, that there seems quite some disagreement between the Office of the Prosecution and amici curiae and also the Croatian government. What I just heard was that you repeated your position but without responding to the reasons why the amici and the Croatian government have some doubts as to whether there could be a direct application of norms of international law. Could Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you elaborate on that, apart from repeating your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I did anticipate we would eventually if not now get into that in a larger and much more detailed way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would like to do it at a later stage --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm happy, Your Honour to say that it seems to me, particularly in connection with the issue of command responsibility, which is an issue in the case, and whether there is a Croatian substitute or way to address, to sufficiently address, adequately address command responsibility as a theory of prosecution in the Croatian courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do not mind if you would like to address it in relation to the issue of command responsibility, where it appears to be most urgent. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just if I could -- Mr. President, to answer your questions and to preview the further discussion, it seems to us that the amici in the state of Croatia would prefer, I think on balance, to find a solution to the problem in Croatian national domestic law by pulling certain statutes under the general criminal code and attempting to press those statutes into service to accomplish some form of what we would call at the Tribunal 7(3) or command responsibility. On balance, the Prosecution's view, and I think it's firmed up some since we filed our submissions some days ago: We would view and would submit today for the Chamber's consider that international law, the application of international law provides a more reliable and more predictable basis to address these matters under -- because -- and again as a preview, based upon Croatia's full acceptance of the Geneva Conventions, including Protocol 1 which was in force at the time and based on customary international law including the customary law of command responsibility, as recognised by the Hadzihasanovic interlocutory appeal decision. We do have some concerns, Mr. President, about some of the applications of domestic law. And again, that gets us into these various questions such as mens rea. And indirect intent and advertent negligence and again, topics that will be discussed more in the course of the day. Let me order the time that's been allowed me, Your Honour; let me see if there's any other additional comments that I might be able to make at this time. Unless the Court has additional questions I think I would just conclude for now by saying: Again, the Prosecution on balance has considered these matters and looked at the existing indictment, has looked at Croatian law and international law; and while it would be dishonest to say that we have no concerns about these issues, that there are some legitimate issues that are before the Chamber, on balance, once again, we think there is a basis for a fully appropriate prosecution in Croatia, again, in the conditions of the specialised courts that have been set up and the legislation -- the new legislation and reforms that have been adopted. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then proceed and give an opportunity to the Defence for Mr. Ademi to address the Court. Mr. Prodanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, distinguished colleagues of the Prosecution, and my colleagues present here, representatives of the government, or the amicus curiae rather. First of all, let me start off by saying that as a general stand, as a general position, the Defence of General Ademi agrees with the proposition made by the Prosecution that the Ademi/Norac case be referred to Croatia first and foremost guided by the new strategy, the completion strategy, and of course everything that we have heard to date and on the basis of resolution of 2003, Resolution 1503. Although I don't wish to repeat what the Prosecution has said or follow their order, I will have to do to a certain measure. Of course, before this Court, before this Tribunal, we had the trials of crimes that were of less gravity -- of course there are no crimes of less gravity before this Tribunal, but if we speak in relative terms, then we will have to do that and call them that. And of course, people were tried -- accused were tried of a lower rank, either by virtue of rank or by virtue of their military hierarchy position. However, if we are guided by the criteria which are present and conditioned by the circumstances put forward by the Prosecution, that is to say the awareness that physically speaking not all trials can be tried and completed by this Tribunal, then, as we have stated, we consider that this particular trial falls under the criteria set out which would satisfy the referral of this trial to the Croatian legislature. Why? Because in our opinion along with the proviso that I've already said that there are no less grave or more grave crimes and that of course the accused have held this intermediate rank and responsibility, they are still not the highest ranking officials, whether political or military, that stand accused before this Tribunal appeared that were tried by this Tribunal, and therefore come under these criteria. Now, this introduction of mine speaks in one way of an ambivalence in the relationship and position taken which was expressed by the Prosecution a moment ago: on the one hand the awareness that we are dealing with serious crimes, grave crimes; that we are dealing with accused persons who do have a level of responsibility and held a certain position; and also of the awareness of the fact that these matters cannot be dealt with within the frameworks and time frame of this Tribunal and that we will have to find another solution, the solution that was discussed and set out a moment ago. With respect to Rule 11 bis being applied of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence with all the provisos that I've also mentioned. When we speak of all the crimes, the Defence which does not agree with all the assertions made by the Prosecution in the indictment, and these will be questions which we shall deal with in due course, does consider that we are nonetheless dealing here with a militarily justified action in a narrow period, in a short space of time where the number of victims -- there was a number of victims which we know, but we do not know whether those victims fell victim on the basis of unlawful action by the accused or whether they were the results of military actions by the accused or whether they were the results of military action, that is to say battles and fighting. So these are matters which remain open questions and will have to be deliberated. At the same time, with respect to the level of responsibility or positions held by persons concerned, namely General Ademi, the Defence will repeat its, reiterate its stand, which it presented in its motion and submission, and that is that he never de facto had effective control over all the units during the operation. In the submission by the Prosecution, we were in a way criticised that we spoke about his rank and that we delved into factual debate about that. But I think that it is impossible without entering into a factual debate to speak about ranks and positions of the accused in this particular operation and for the material time, that is to say the Medak Pocket 1993, because he functioned in an interaction and correlation with other accused, or rather with other individuals. And we claimed - and in an implicit way this was confirmed by the conduct of the Prosecution as well - that the accused Ademi at the material time was not the highest ranking military officer in the territory while the operation was taking place. While the operation was taking place, there were four generals in that area, each of them having their own specific function, actively participating and highly involved in the determination and implementation of the operation itself. So the Prosecution in a way accepted these arguments of ours and this is borne out of the fact that General Bobetko was accused for the same operation as an individual who conceived, planned, and commanded the operation; and that simultaneously, in relation to that operation, investigations were conducted against two other suspects, two other generals of the Croatian army who at that time were in the Medak Pocket and each of them in their own way played a certain part in the operation. Let me summarise. At the time brigadier or as the speaker says as major general was only in formal terms the commander of the operation, de jure he did have certain control over the units, but because of the fact that the operation was planned by the Main Staff, which can be seen from the book written by General Bobetko. And when the operation was implemented General Ademi was skipped over and there was direct communication with lower units in the field without the knowledge of General Ademi. We claim and we submit that he at no event -- in no event was the individual who was the alpha and omega of this action, which he is being accused of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic, I do understand that in order to assess the gravity of the crimes and the level of responsibility, that sticking literally to the text of the indictment might not give a -- could not lead to a proper interpretation of what your client is charged with. On the other hand, if we go too much into details of facts, the merits of the case itself -- this Court has not read a book written by Mr. Bobetko. This Court, this Chamber, has not heard any evidence on that. And the gist of the referral is that these matters will be determined if a referral will take place, by the Court. So would you please limit yourself in dealing with matters of fact at this moment and concentrate on what is really necessary to make a determination on the gravity of the crimes and the level of responsibility as charged. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have completed the facts -- with the facts; I have dealt with them. And I said that quite simply I wanted to set this out without -- and the Prosecutor has read General Bobetko, but I'm also clear that there are no criteria, legal criteria, on the basis of which we can determine the gravity of a crime because there is no differentiated span of sentences of the international criminal court. So we tried to use some auxiliary criteria in order to help us and to further our position, which is that we consider that they were crimes of such -- on such a scale that they can be backed in this way. So that is what I wanted to say with regard to the gravity of the crime and the level of responsibility of the accused General Ademi. With respect to the legal framework for proceedings to be conducted, the Defence would like to join in the representative -- join in what the amicus curiae stated and the government representative stated that the basis for the proceeding for the aspects of substantive law is the criminal code dating back to 1993, first of all guided by the principle of legality and no retroactive measures. This afternoon as far as I was able to see from our schedule for today, there will be a lot of discussion on the subject of finding legal means and remedies and legal means for the trial. I would like to say that legal means do exist for a trial to take place pursuant to the provisions and rules of the Republic of Croatia by which a certain problem of a command responsibility and everything derived from that, from para 7 of the Statute can be bridged in the way we have presented in the legal opinions of the representatives of the government or the amicus curiae, and that is with respect to -- the failure to prevent a crime must be looked at and the perpetration of crimes that the provisions of the criminal code should be applied, as prescribed by the 1993 criminal code, which means that once a crime has been committed the perpetrators must be brought to justice. Also, I wish to draw your attention to Article 18 of the penal code which makes it possible to apply directly international conventions if certain legal situations are not regulated by the provisions of national law. I see that my time is running out, so I will expound our responses in the most concise possible way to the questions put by Your Honours. The courts in the Republic of Croatia have already proceeded applying the regulations in the way described. And I would especially wish to draw your attention to the trial of Dinko Sakic who had been the commander of the Jasenovac Ustasha camp and who was tried for failure to punish his subordinates who had perpetrated crimes in the Jasenovac camp. With respect to the possible problem of providing protection for victims and witnesses, all I can say is that in Croatia this has been provided for relatively well through three laws, the law on criminal procedure, the police law, and other legislation. And we have elaborated on this in detail in our written submission, so I will not belabour the point. Also, there is a commission that has been set up for the protection of witnesses and a judge of the Supreme Court of Croatia has been nominated as the head of that commission. I am aware that there are certain fears that victims' and witness' protection will not be able to be fully implemented, in other words that there are certain risks and even dangers, but I do not believe that this will diverge significantly from the measures provided for by the ICTY. As for international legal aid, there is an entire section in the law on criminal procedure regulating international legal assistance. International legal aid has been used in many cases in Croatia when calling witnesses or taking written statements. And there will be other such cases in future, as due to the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia there are many witnesses outside the jurisdiction of the Croatia courts. Therefore these methods have been set up and they are functioning well and legal aid is being provided internationally. My learned friend has touched upon the report of the OSCE on their monitoring of criminal proceedings pertaining to war times in the Republic of Croatia. This report gives a picture of the Croatian judiciary which is not very favourable, but in our view this picture is partially distorted due to the fact that monitoring covered a period of ten years and most of the objections are made to the first years when the Croatian judiciary was not at its best. However, we feel that today the situation is much better and that apart from several proceedings which exemplify not properly conducted trials in Croatia, these have been publicly condemned and overturned by the Supreme Court. There are other examples where trials have been conducted properly and have met the highest standards of the international community. President Meron has expressed a favourable opinion of the current situation, and therefore I believe that the transfer of one case will not be a problem for the Croatian judiciary and that the Croatian judiciary will deal with it properly, as has been the case in the Gospic case, which we are all aware of. I believe that my time has run out and I hope I have managed to put forward the points I felt necessary to raise today. And in agreement with the Prosecutor, we feel that there should be no problems and that although of course there are risks, we believe these can all be overcome successfully in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic, you referred to Article 18 of the criminal code of Croatia in relation to the application of international law. I'm not sure the Chamber has the full Article of that penal code. Could you read out that -- that provision of criminal code.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite honest, Your Honour, I mentioned that article. I don't have the text of the criminal code before me, but reading the comments of other authors and checking this in the legislation I quoted it; however, I don't have it before me right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell us what is the crux of the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The crux is in that if certain crimes are not listed as special crimes in the criminal code of the Republic of Croatia, then the international conventions pertaining to this can be applied directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- I see that both the representatives of the government and amici curiae are busy and trying to find the text. Mr. Prodanovic, I take it that you would gladly accept the assistance of the representatives of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we be informed about the literal text of Article 18. You referred especially to paragraph 2 in your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not Article 18 that is being mentioned here. We should be aware of the fact that we have two criminal laws, one which was in force when the alleged crimes were committed for which the accused Ademi and Norac, that they are charged with. That is the law of 1993. And a law in force from the 1st of January, 1998, the new criminal code. It cannot be applied retroactively to this case, but the principles of the new legislation, whereby international law is considered to be a source of Croatian law, these principles will be applied to every trial for crimes committed prior to the entry into force of that law, because of the rule of law. This is not Article 18; this is the general principle underlying that legislation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Horvatic, of course at a later stage you will be given an opportunity to explain the position of the government you're representing, but at this moment we are just about to find the text Mr. Prodanovic is referring to. Mr. Prodanovic, I must say that in your written submission it's a bit of a general problem, the sources of the positions you defend in your written submissions. But the Chamber would really like to receive from you the text you're referring to, both in your written submission, Article 18, paragraph 2, as you repeated it in your oral submission today, you refer to Article 18. We'd like to receive the text of what you're referring to. Would it be possible, perhaps, that you find it during the next break?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'm afraid not now. Maybe -- I'll try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it it must be possible one way or the other to provide it to us today, because it might be an important element in further submissions, so therefore we would like to be informed about this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The passage appears on page 4 of your submission dated 3rd of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Prodanovic, thank you for your submissions. Would there be anything you would like to add or -- because you're afraid that you'll run out of time. Not yet, but if you say I'm finished --

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: You gave me 20 minutes as far as I know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you look at the clock you're not running out of time; if you look at the time consumed, then you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, I have finished, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, may I invite you to make submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I wish to thank my learned friends as well and greet all those present in the courtroom, the representatives of the Republic of Croatia, the amici curiae, and my colleagues from the Defence. We have already seen during the introductory remarks of my learned friends, as well as the Defence, that it is very difficult, Your Honours, when debating an issue such as the one we are debating today not to touch upon the facts with regard to the alleged crimes in the indictment. Of course I will try to avoid this, but I do have to touch upon the submissions of my learned friends, when Mr. Scott said that this case could be tried either before the ICTY or before the courts in Croatia. With all due respect, I consider this to be a rhetorical device because what we are dealing with here today is a case initiated by the Prosecution for which the Prosecution moves that it be tried in Croatia. The fears expressed by my learned friends about the courts in Croatia are not justified. If the Prosecution wants the best prosecutors to prosecute this case, that will be done; but we also need the best defence counsel as well because we all want the truth to be properly established. We all know that according to the terms of 11 bis, there is not only the possibility of monitoring the trial at any time, but also that the case may be brought back to the Tribunal, should it be established that anything was being done that was not in accordance with the law. I'm certain, however, that the intention behind this provision is that no trial should be conducted to the detriment of the accused. Speaking hypothetically, the rights of the defence might be violated and this, too, would be a cause for returning the case of the ICTY. Your Honours, you already have a certain guarantee. Although we as the Defence fully support the Prosecution motion, as can be seen from our entire correspondence with the Tribunal and all our motions that have been submitted. But in any case we are deeply convinced that the Chamber Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the Republic of Croatia will be fully objective [as interpreted], should Your Honours decide to refer the case to Croatia. Your Honours, we are absolutely certain that the Chamber in Croatia will not be favourably disposed toward my client, as my client has already been sentenced to 12 years in prison, as has been decided by the appellate court. And this is one of the arguments that Your Honours will certainly consider when you deliberate your decision. By your leave, Your Honours, I wish to briefly touch upon the command responsibility of my client, or rather his level of responsibility because I feel that the Prosecution has not sufficiently described the position of my client. As the Prosecution has done, of course this should be described in two ways, but they have not drawn a sufficient distinction between military rank on the one hand and the command role in the tempore criminus suspecti that my client had. With all due respect for my learned friends, I don't think we should confuse the position of my client, Mr. Mirko Norac, who was a colonel at the time -- we should not confuse his position with the position that that rank normally holds in other armies. The Defence has studied the ranks in the army from the rank of colonel to that of general. Between colonel and general there are also brigadier and staff brigadier. So when we look at the hierarchy we see that staff brigadier and brigadier come above colonel and major in the Croatian army. The ranks in the Croatian army, therefore, in comparison to the hierarchy in Western armies were stozerni general, Field Marshal General Zbora, General; General Pukovnik, major general; and General Potpukovnik, lieutenant general and general major brigadier.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This is the Defence translation of the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of Brigadier Ademi at that time has also not been properly clarified with all the other superiors, for example the position of General Bobetko who was directly under the command of the Minister of Defence. Between the Minister of Defence and Brigadier Ademi, there were a number of generals and staff brigadiers, not to mention this relationship with regard to Colonel Norac. As regards the Prosecution position, there is no dispute, of course, that the Security Council issued Resolution 1534 and that pursuant to this resolution this special Chamber understands this resolution to be an instruction regarding the criteria to be applied. For example, in the Aleksovski case, regardless of military rank, this would no longer be tried by this Tribunal pursuant to Resolution 1534. Therefore, I feel there is no need to look back but to look at the motions before you at the present time in the light of Resolution 1534 and that doing this, Your Honours, will certainly decide that this is a case that can be transferred or referred to the courts in Croatia. Your Honour, in response to the questions you have put to the Defence, your first question was: What is the relevant law applicable to this case, whether the law of 1993 or the criminal code of 2004? In the view of the Defence, there can be no dilemma. The law to be applied is the one tempore criminus suspecti. That is the one most favourable to the accused. Therefore, in view of the Defence, and I see this is also the position of the Republic of Croatia and the amici curiae, it is the law of 1993 that should be applied because the penal system of the Republic of Croatia and of all continental law, all this is based on nullum crimen sine lege and nulla pena sine lege. However, the Defence considers that this legal issue should not play a crucial role when deciding whether or not that refer this case to the Republic of Croatia. Should you so decide what will be important is for the proceedings to be conducted strictly in accordance with the law and that the Chamber when reaching its decision, whether of sentence or acquittal, should do so in accordance with the law. The second question was what forms of protection are available for victims and witnesses in Croatia and on the basis of what such measures would be granted. Your Honour, let me again refer to the proceedings I participated in in Croatia where General Norac was accused and sentenced to 12 years in prison, which is a very high sentence. At a trial there were dozens of witnesses from Serbia and Montenegro who has nothing specific to say about the indictment but who testified before the Chamber, and there were no problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, you have given similar observations in your written submissions where you're criticising the proceedings in the earlier case against Mr. Norac, and that's not a matter that we can deal with at this moment; whether a witness in that proceedings has lied or has not lied is totally beyond what this Chamber can deal with. I think it should even not have been adopted in your written submissions, but certainly a repetition in this oral hearing is not appropriate. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be brief, I think that in any case supporting what my learned friends have put forward in their motion after Your Honours hear the arguments of the amici curiae and the representatives of the Republic of Croatia, this case has all the components needed for Your Honours to refer it without any reservations to the Republic of Croatia, which will conduct the proceedings against Mr. Norac and Mr. Ademi in accordance with the law. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to give an opportunity to the Bench to ask any further I would say clarifying questions at this moment, so not perhaps to go into every detail, but... Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, just this observation: You mentioned the possibility on the part of the Croatian court of the application of international law, inter alia the Geneva Conventions Protocol 1. And you also expressed some concerns about some of the applications of domestic laws in such areas as mens rea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it that you are making -- the Prosecution is making this request conditional upon the answers to such questions? And if you make your position be known to the parties, the Chamber will be assisted by hearing the responses of the -- from the Croatian government and amicus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour Judge Kwon. The Prosecution assesses the current indictment, the case against these accused, by not hinging entirely by any means on what we would call command responsibility or 7(3) responsibility. Having said that, we would consider that it is an important component of any successful -- likely-to-succeed, if I can put it that way, prosecution that we would want to or I think any prudent prosecutor at the ICTY or in Croatia would want to have available to him or her the theory of command responsibility as practiced internationally and at the ICTY. Included in that is the practice of the ICTY, the jurisprudence of the ICTY that allows a successful prosecution, if you will, based on a had-to-reason-to-know standard. And that gets us into these issues of mens rea that, Judge Kwon, you just raised and are featured in the papers. Before I turn to discuss the mens rea issue further, let's come back to what I think your question is: Yes. I think the Prosecution view is that at the end of the day if neither the Prosecution nor the Bench was sufficiently confident that a Prosecution in Croatia would be able to find some basis, some reliable, firm basis for a command responsibility component, then I think it would raise questions about whether the case should be transferred. So, yes, in that sense I think -- I wouldn't say our position is conditional, but we have made the assessment and we think, our assessment is the best answer is international law. But we have made the assessment that there is a basis -- there would be a basis for such a prosecution in Croatia and that's why we go forward with our motion. But I would agree, I think as I understand your question, Judge Kwon, if again -- sorry, I'm repeating myself. If at the end of the day there was a question about that, I think it would be a serious consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few question for you, Mr. Scott, since you are on your feet anyhow. May I draw you to page 2 of your last submission, that is the Further Submission Pursuant to Chamber's Order of the 20th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Prosecution's submission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's on page 2 and it's the 7th... I tried to understand your observations in view of Article 28, paragraph 2. It reads: "Article 28, paragraph 2, indicates that a failure to prevent liability exists if there is a legal duty to prevent the prohibited consequence, 'if such failure in acts and meaning is identical to the commission of the crime by acting.'" I tried to understand this sentence. I've got two questions. First we have two times, if there is a cumulative test, if there is a legal duty to prohibit a legal consequence, if such failure and meaning is identical to the commission of crime by acting. My second question would be: A failure to act is by its very nature not the same as acting; that's the reason why we need legal constructions to cover these situations. But in this last part of the sentence I read: "If such failure and acts and meaning is identical to the commission of the crime by acting." You say if it's the same then it's the same. Then we're trying to deal with differences. Could you please clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I will attempt to do so, Your Honour. I think the language is taken from a translation of Article 28 itself as far as I understand it. So perhaps part of it is an issue of translation or part of it's just a wording of the Croatian statute. But be that as it may, there is of course omission -- an omission I think in most systems, I hazard to say, and including in Croatia, an omission is only criminal if the person who failed to act, who omitted to act had a duty to act in some fashion otherwise. You had -- he or she had a duty to do Z and didn't do Z, omitted to do Z. And in that sense there is a failure to do something that the law or some code required him or her to do, and that is the nature of the offence. I think in terms of the language it talks about: "If such failure in acts and meaning is identical to the commission of the crime by acting," I interpret that, and I stand to be corrected by my friends from the Republic of Croatia and amici, I interpret that to basically mean one who participates, again, in a commission of a crime by failing to prevent in some sense has in some sense a responsibility identical to the one who actually commits the crime, which I don't think is a necessarily unusual concept here, such as aiding and abetting or co-perpetration or members of a joint criminal enterprise, to use that terminology. If one contributes to the crime, in this case by contributing by failure to prevent, one becomes essentially responsibility [sic] identical to the actual, on-the-ground perpetrators, as it were. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, there is an if. So that means that not all failure is supposed to be identical. Then of course the legal issue is: When yes? When no? That's the problem. As I said before, it reads a bit like if it's true, then it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. And again, I'm not -- I'll stand to be corrected by my Croatian colleagues. I think that's the wording of the statute, but I can't be in the position of defending the words of the Croatian statute. I think that is one of the issues and in fact that's what lead us -- that's a number of factors that lead us away, if you will, from relying on finding answers in domestic law, why we prefer and we feel that international law is a clear and firmer foundation for this. Related to that -- sorry, Judge Orie, to respond further to your question I think and it relates partly to what you're saying: Is there a duty to act or not and not all failures are necessarily criminal. That then takes us back into the mens rea question. And there again, unless an adequate -- unless we can get to a point that we feel comfortable that there's some mens rea in Croatian law that is comparable to the Tribunal law, then once again we would not feel confident in relying on that. And that applies to the various Croatian statutes that have been cited by Croatia and amici. It seems to be the position that there is no basis for any negligence or any crimes committed by negligence under Croatian law, and then of course that takes us into this issue of advertent and inadvertent negligence. I note that, but at the same time there is a statute which specifically talks about negligence being the basis of criminal law and maybe counsel would like to address that. But that is the set of issues, 4 those are the types of issues that could lead us to have some doubts on which this is a firm basis for us to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you seem to struggle a bit more with Article 28 because Article 28 paragraph 3 is mentioned in paragraph 11, page 4 of your -- of this same written submission. Can you give us one interpretation, of course that's always -- raises the issue what the other interpretation would be. But foremost what the text of Article 28 would be. So 18 for the Defence, perhaps 28 for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think I have and I can certainly provide it, but I think I have it with me. We can provide it of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can please do that. This might not be all of my questions, but the first break was scheduled for 10.00. We'll have a break first. We might have a few more questions after the break to the parties, but once we have heard the parties we are -- the next step will be hear the submissions by the amicus curiae and by the Croatian government. We'll adjourn until 10.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume the hearing and I would have a few more questions. First of all, Mr. Prodanovic, is Article 18 already available or is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm afraid I won't be able to tell you too much at this point because in our desire to illustrate one of the exceptions from the principle of legality, provided an example with legal theory mentioned in one point in an official article. But in talking about it to the professors a moment ago, they consider that it isn't a very good example for this particular instance and situation, so that therefore, I am going to give up on what I said in a little -- in a manner that wasn't critical enough and I will be guided by them. So this was just by way of illustration, that there is the legal source and deviation from the principle of legality, but perhaps I didn't pick the best possible example for the case in point regarding legality for our point in brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was the only example you gave. If you would have any other -- if you say it's not the best example, we'll do with the second best, if you provide to it us. If you do not do that, we have no example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Scott, after 18 now 28, do you have a text?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour. It's not my position to speak for counsel on the other side or alter their position. We do have a copy of Article 18, be whatever counsel's position is, whether it's a good example or not, we're happy to provide it. We're not commenting on counsel's position, just to provide what we believe a copy of the Statute to the Chamber. We also have provided a copy of Article 28 and I understand in talking to the representative from the Republic of Croatia that the second "if" apparently has been removed at some point from the legislation and he's able to clarify that more specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll hear on that at a later stage. I also do understand whether it's the best example or not, the Article 18 that has been provided to us at this moment first of all is adopted after the 1993 code, as far as I understand, and it's limited to statutory limitation and not on the positive application of provisions of a criminal nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's what it appears, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we'll ignore it if you consider it not to be a good example. We'll just ignore it until you have come up with a better example. Yes. Then perhaps -- yes, Mr. Scott, I think there's one issue and I again do not insist on an immediate answer, but it turns out to be rather vital it seems -- well, vital. At least it keeps government amici and the OTP apart where we would expect that if you're confident that you can refer a case, then at least on the basic issues you would take the same view. The issue of direct application of international law, be it treaty law or be it customary law, in -- by a local court. First of all I wonder whether we should not make a distinction on whether a state is bound by obligations it has accepted in treaties or even if not accepted, bound by customary international law, general principles of international law and whether courts could directly apply treaty provisions and/or customary law. I just read to you an order - not because it's the answer, but at least it clearly poses the problem. The former president of this institution wrote a book on international criminal law and he says the following: "Normally national courts do not undertake proceedings for international crimes only on the basis of international customary law; that is, if a crime is only provided for in that body of law. They instead tend to require either a national statute defining crime and grant national courts jurisdiction over it, or if a treaty has been ratified on the matter by that state, the passing of implementing legislation, enabling courts to fully provide the relevant treaty provisions." That's on page 303. On page 305 he says this phenomena is all the more serious "because national courts are not prepared to exercise jurisdiction if express national legislation to this effect is lacking." In your submission you said not only that Croatia can - I understand this to be Croatian courts - can but also should apply international law. You gave no authorities for that and from what the Chamber understands, the monistic or the dualistic approach in relation to international law and domestic law is usually governed by rules of constitutional law. The difference is in one country one would take a very strict monistic approach, in which always the transformation under all circumstances for all parts of international law would be needed, whereas in other systems either a direct applicability of international law or a treaty is provided for in the constitutional system. For example, in the German constitutional system, from what I remember, general principles of international law can be directly applied; treaty provisions, however, under German law are not directly applicable in German courts. This is just an example. But that's where the problem might lie. And until now you have expressed several times your preference for finding the solution in international law but you have not explained how under Croatian constitutional law this would be possible, and in this respect the OTP takes a position quite different from the representatives of the government and of amicus and even if not immediate -- the matter should be further addressed by the OTP. I have a few more questions for you. On page 7 of your submission you take the position - and that's a position taken also by Defence counsel, at least one of them - that ancillary orders could be given by the Tribunal which seems to indicate that a referral in your view would not mean that the Tribunal is totally out of the picture until the moment that it has applied for the case to be referred again to the Tribunal. But could you briefly explain what in your view still is the role of the Tribunal in, for example, securing international cooperation in criminal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll try to do that. I think that that paragraph 18 of our submission, if I can characterise it as such, was frankly a bit of thinking out loud. This whole regime of 11 bis and how it relates to other parts of the Statute and other procedures, such as request for state assistance, potentially binding orders, subpoenas, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. summons, et cetera, when you wrap all that together, it just occurred to us that it might - and I think that's all we really said was might - provide a basis that if there was some gap in the procedural law or the aspects of interstate cooperation in particular that for some reason, and I'm just simply picking an example off the top of my head, Croatia couldn't get some needed assistance from Serbia and Montenegro, that perhaps the Tribunal might be in a position as some sort of, I suppose, middleman to assist in using its tools to provide some assistance if it could not be accomplished otherwise. But to be very transparent, again, that was just basically thinking that that might be possible, if the situation arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mediation is not the same as, as you used it, ancillary orders. The Defence used the terminology also of mediation. Is it the position of the OTP that the Tribunal, even if the case is still referred and not taken back, that it could exercise any powers under -- well, as a consequence of its establishment under chapter 7 of the United Nations Charter? Have we given up the power or do we still have it? Apart from the power to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It seems to me, Your Honours, particularly with the states of the former Yugoslavia which I think stand in a special relation to the Tribunal, and if there were some problem that the Tribunal could assist with -- I was just looking for some examples. You have Rule 54, the general rule; Rule 54 bis, orders direct to states. There might be a vehicle and perhaps not. There might be some way that if Croatia were to come back to the Tribunal and say: This case has been transferred to us, however we're having a problem getting this evidence from Serbia. Might the Tribunal be able to issue some orders or to assist us or mediate and/or issue some orders that would allow us to get that material if it couldn't be obtained, for instance, through a mutual assistance treaty. Again, it was basically trying to be creative and thinking if there are ways to solve problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One difficulty I see there, Mr. Scott, is that the powers available to this Tribunal would normally be understood I think as in aid of its exercise of its jurisdiction and the situation we're dealing with is predicated with on this Tribunal having referred the case to the court of another state. I would say that we may not have a jurisdictional foundation to make any order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Parker, I think your point is well taken. It may not be -- again, we're all writing on a bit of a clean slate under 11 bis. I think an argument can be made and perhaps the Chamber would disagree, but an argument could be made under 11 bis that it seems to anticipate or provide for by implication the continuing monitoring and oversight of the proceeding. When you look at some of the rules like (F) and (G) it talks about the case being withdrawn. I think there is some sense there that there is some continuing oversight. I hate to use the word jurisdiction, but there is some continuing jurisdiction in the sense of the continuing ability to intervene and pull the case back. I think the Statute -- the rule provides for that. In that sense, if you say in that context that the Chamber or the Tribunal provides jurisdiction at least to that limited extent, then one can make the argument that any such arguments would be in assistance or ancillary to its jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me put that question quite sharp to you. Mr. Scott, if the OTP would be of the opinion that the case would be prosecuted far better if Witness X would be appear and if the Prosecution, local Prosecution would not call that witness, could the Prosecution ask for an order by the Tribunal to call a witness in the local proceedings? I mean, you're more or less presenting a position where you say: Since we still have the power to call the case back to The Hague, other powers of, minor powers, could be exercised. If you say we could call the case back and hear that witness here, so why should we not exercise our powers to instruct the prosecution in Croatia to call a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I see the Court's point. I think one can argue that if you have a power to do a lot, you have power to do something less. If the Chamber has the power to withdraw the case entirely, the argument can be made why can't they intervene in some other way as well. It's an all-or-nothing approach. It's a situation where the Tribunal would do nothing to intervene until it observes something that was so unacceptable that we're simply going to call the whole case back, and we wait until we got to that stage, or whether it would have the ability to intervene more episodically to say this is a problem that needs to be addressed. But Your Honour, I have to say again, this is uncharted territory and we just thought that there might be some means for the Tribunal to assist in this way. But other people may take the view once the case is transferred, it's completely gone. Even in that view, Rule subpart (F) clearly provides for the possibility of bringing it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's for sure. I think at a later stage we'll hear from the Croatian government how it perceives its loss of autonomy as presented by the Prosecution in this moment. One more question, Mr. Scott. Does the Prosecution take it, because on page 7 of the last submission you have given an impression on what kind of material you would send. Would the Prosecution consider its obligation to disclose any exculpatory material still existent even if the case is referred?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course. I think that runs as our responsibility to the case as a whole. I think that's an ethical obligation we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you would send that to the court to which the case is referred and not directly to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would assume it would depend on the system; if you have an investigating judge or a prosecutor, we would probably send it either to the prosecutor or the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It also depends on the -- yes. Then perhaps one final question. You are, on page 10 of your submission, in some dispute about whether responsibility, command responsibility is -- well, the same as a direct individual responsibility and you say, no, there's no difference in level; it's all the same as far as gravity is concerned, there's no principal distinction. This draws my attention to the fact that in footnote 9 we find the penalties that could be imposed for command responsibility under the present law not applicable. But the one to five years and one to eight years, depending on the variety -- depending on the form of 7(3) responsibility, clearly express a far lower level of punishment. So therefore I see there is some difference of view on whether it's an equal level or a difference of level. My question is: Mainly do you expect the Croatian courts to follow their tradition as expressed in the new legislation, which means a far lower level of criminal responsibility in terms of punishment, or would you expect them to apply or to follow your interpretation that 7(3) responsibility is of a similar gravity, similar level than the 7(1)?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Orie, I really wouldn't expect the Croatian judiciary to pay much attention to my opinion one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whether it would be advisable or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think the crucial point is that the Statute does seem to provide for much less of a sentence it would apply here and that would cause us some concern. That takes us back perhaps a bit into the direct application of international law question. I suppose if the Croatian judges were to apply international law, then perhaps they also would look to fashion a sentence consistent with international law. But I do see the discrepancy, and of course, Judge Orie, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answers, Mr. Scott. Let me just have a look at whether I have any additional questions for the Defence. Yes. We've heard a lot. Mr. Olujic, you presented the whole military hierarchy ranks, et cetera, whereas everyone may have seen on the -- on our screen we received the message that the interpreters had some difficulties in following the ranks and translating them and they asked our attention to that. May I just ask you in a totally different way, perhaps, this same question: How many troops in your view - and I don't know whether there's any disagreement between your views and the Prosecution - how many troops were under the command of your client, Mr. Norac, at the relevant time, which is the Croatian Medak Pocket?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At present I cannot say. But in any case it was his motorised brigade and no one else that was under his command. Otherwise, we would be entering into the territory of other units and special units taking part in the operation. He was commanding his own regiment and the number of troops at the tempore criminus suspecti I cannot tell you, Your Honour, at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. It seems, Mr. Olujic, that in your last submission on page 2 that you take more or less the view that we should strictly adhere to the principle of non-retroactivity. That would mean that the outcome is of no importance for the referral. That would mean, but please correct me if I understand you wrongly, that it is already clear at this moment that certain behaviours and conducts would not be covered by the applicable substantive Croatian law, that we nevertheless should refer the case to Croatia and then head for an almost inevitable acquittal. Is that what your position is?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. In my view, the entire indictment and everything being alleged can and does fall under Croatian legislation and its provisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even command responsibility, in the specific form of not punishing if you not only have known but if you should have known that the crimes were about to be committed or that the crimes were committed? That would still fall, in your view, under the Croatian law applicable in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. I think yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would perhaps further today -- if you would like to further elaborate on the basis for this position, that certainly would assist the Chamber. These were my questions for the moment. Then I'd like to give an opportunity to Amicus Curiae Professor Krapac, to address the Chamber and to submit whatever you would like to submit in addition to the brief that has been filed by you and Professor Damaska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- there's a good tradition in this Tribunal if there's no lectern for someone so he breaks his back, more or less, that it's provided by whoever has one available. If you would like to have something more higher up --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [In English] No, I'm comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're comfortable. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, allow me at the outset to thank you on behalf of Professor Damaska and on my own behalf on your decision in allowing us to appear here as amicus curiae. As you know Professor Damaska is one of the prominent experts in the field of comparative penal and criminal law and international criminal law and for many years now he has dealt with issues of international criminal law. And I myself have for a considerable time been observing the efforts of the legal community to contribute through international criminal justice to criminal law and the rule of law and to contribute to the goals enshrined in the ICTY Statute. Today I can speak with only one voice because Professor Damaska was unable to attend for reasons of health, and therefore I can either speak louder or I can speak longer than I would if I was speaking only on my own behalf. That is why I ask you for a little patience. We have made our submission as amici curiae and its content fall into three basic headings: First, whether this case is suitable for referral to the Croatian authorities; secondly, whether the Croatian legislation provides a sufficient normative basis for successful trial and for due process; and what operative problems might arise in the cooperation between the Croatian judiciary and the Prosecution of this Tribunal. At the outset I can say that the first of these issues has been, at least as far as I am concerned, one of the most difficult issues we have tried to resolve: the issue of the level of the accused in this case and their criminal responsibility. And the response to this question represents a precedent. We have attempted to find a solution in a letter sent by the President of the International Criminal Tribunal of Rwanda of the Security Council in May of last year. Therein he lists a combination of criteria of what should be taken into account when deciding on whether a certain case is to be retained or transferred, or rather referred, to the national judiciaries. The criteria listed are as follows. I quote in English: [In English] The alleged status of the individual during the crimes committed; the alleged connection an individual might have with other cases; the need to cover the major geographical areas in which the crimes were allegedly committed; the availability of evidence with regard to the individual concerned; the concrete possibility of arresting the individual concerned and the availability of investigative material for transmission to a state for national prosecution."
