[Interpretation] So this is a series of criteria which cannot be applied automatically in the present case but which may serve as inspiration when considering how such a decision might be made. We are aware, of course, that the greatest difficulty in the application and identification of these criteria is the difficulty faced by the Prosecution. Of all the parties to this case, the Prosecution is the best informed concerning the specific circumstances falling under the above-mentioned criteria, and they are able to decide on the level of responsibility and the gravity of the crimes in this case. As we have heard from Mr. Scott today, the Prosecution has compiled a comparative table to demonstrate the gravity of crimes and the level of responsibility. As for the gravity of the crimes, I think that perhaps the best way to demonstrate this is to refer to a statement made by the chief prosecutor, Mrs. Del Ponte, before the Security Council in which she says that this Tribunal, in her view, must retain within its jurisdiction all cases against perpetrators who have committed the most serious crimes falling within its jurisdiction and which, I quote in English -- [In English] "Criminal plan fervently put into action in the area and had blood on their own hands," [Interpretation] referring to their criminal plan. This metaphor is perhaps the best way of expressing what the letter from the President of the Rwanda Tribunal mentions, enumerating the criteria that should guide the Chamber in deciding which cases to refer to national jurisdictions. With reference to these criteria, we have concluded that the criteria of a connection between this case and the courts in the Republic of Croatia could be an argument supporting referral because hearing the case on the territory of the Republic of Croatia would make it possible for what is usually said to constitute an easier communication between the court and the local population. I will not go into the details of what this means. It would make it easier to prove certain facts in relation to both of the accused, both with reference to the crimes alleged against them and with reference to their personal family circumstances, their actions and behaviour when carrying out their command duties; and it would facilitate sentencing. And the Chamber would also be aware of the behaviour of the accused in detention, which also must be taken into account during sentencing. Let me also stress that referral of this case would give the greatest possible role in the proceedings to the victims. Compared to some other legislations, the Croatian legislation has given a large role to the victims; they can appear as injured parties in the proceedings with significant rights such as putting forward evidence, investigate -- questioning witnesses and expert witnesses, and even putting forward closing arguments. Not to mention other rights that they have, such as for example claiming damages or appearing as a subsidiary prosecutor in addition to the state prosecutor. As for the second issue, Your Honours, as you have seen we have focused on the issue of command responsibility, or better said, the responsibility of the commander. We are aware of the fact that this is one of the central concepts of international criminal law and that it is thanks to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that this concept has developed significantly. On the other hand, we have to bear in mind that the jurisprudence of this Tribunal in defining and developing the concept of command responsibility and bringing it up to the level of a very sophisticated legal concept has met with misunderstanding in Croatia. Let me mention in passing that it is precisely due to the needs on the national level that the Croatian legislators in their most recent updating of the criminal code have introduced new provisions providing for three types of command responsibility. These are Articles 167(A), subparagraphs 1, 2, and 3. They are not relevant to this case, but I mention them as an illustration of the disposition of the Croatian authorities and the Croatian parliament who wish to solve this issue of command responsibility in accordance with on the one hand the development marked by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and on the other hand in compliance with the national tenets of law. This is of course a matter that Your Honours will deliberate on. The forms of command responsibility which existed under the Croatian criminal legislation of 1993, can these be harmonised or applied in such a way that they are not in disharmony with the demands of the Prosecution which they have put forward today and in their submission of the 7th of February? We have in our written submission identified the contentious issues, and I assume that this is where the Prosecution finds the greatest discrepancies between the concept of command responsibility applied by this Tribunal and command as understood by the Croatian legislation in 1993. We have concluded, however, that these discrepancies are not such that they could not be removed, regardless of whether the solution to this issue is to apply the first of the solutions we proposed, that is applying the norms of international law, the relevant laws of international law which existed even before the Croatian legislation of 1993 or whether this solution is sought through the creative application of the provisions of the law of 1993. To borrow the Prosecutor's phrase: either way, should the accused be found guilty, the concept of command responsibility can be applied in a manner to satisfy the Prosecutor. The third part of our written submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krapac, if you do not mind just dealing with one or two matters that we're dealing with. I found in your amicus brief in footnote 15, a reference to Article 167(A), as you just mentioned. You also on page 21 have provided us with the text of 167(A), and although we are all aware that it is not applicable law, I noticed that on page 21 it seems to be a version of 2003, whereas in footnote 15 you're referring to a version adopted in June 2004. I wondered whether there's any difference between the two texts because if we orient ourselves, even if not applicable, just to understand Croatian law, I would like to avoid whatever confusion might arise, around which version, 2003 or 2004 of Article 167(A).

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is a mistake in the writing. The new legislation was in 2003 and it contained Article 167 (A). However, by a decision of the constitutional code of the Republic of Croatia in November 2003, it was declared formally unconstitutional because when the vote was taken in parliament, a smaller number of deputies than was provided for by the rules voted for it. The new government again initiated the whole process, and this same provision has now entered the legal text because this time parliament carried out the procedure in a proper way. So that the information you have in footnote 15 on page 9 is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Krapac. So the text is the same, but the one was validly adopted, the other one was not validly adopted. I understand the problem. Then -- no, I leave it to that at this very moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will by your leave only briefly address the last part of our submission which is a brief overview of the main characteristics of the criminal judiciary in Croatia. This shows that criminal proceedings have been dealt with exhaustively by the law on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. criminal procedure in 1997, but this is not the only source of criminal procedural law. There are other relevant provisions which would be applied in this case. This is a tradition continental-mixed type of procedure which has provisions on pre-trial proceedings; the issue of the admissibility or inadmissibility of evidence; the division of the roles in the proceedings, and so on and so forth. I will not go into this now, but the fact that all these detailed provisions exist serves to convince us that the Croatian courts are fully able to undertake these proceedings in a way that is referred to as a fair and efficient manner. When compiling our submission, we were conscious of the objections raised against the Croatian judiciary, especially in the earlier period of its activity in the mid and late 1990s. This is a fact which follows from numerous testimonies and is partly referred to in the letter which the representative of the OSCE, Mr. Semneby, addressed to the President of this Tribunal. The facts are also listed in an OSCE report of the spring of last year concerning the situation in the Croatian judiciary. In our view, however, based on previous experience in war-crimes trials, for instance the crimes committed in Gospic which the Defence has referred to today as well as the experience already gained during the trial of Dinko Sakic, which has also been mentioned by the Defence today, based on the fact which counsel for the Prosecution has mentioned today, that is that there are high-quality courts that can easily be identified in Croatia and that the proceedings would be held before the best courts, in our view there should be no doubt that the referred case could be dealt with by the best Croatian courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you mind if I interrupted there, Professor. I've tried to see what is the legislative scheme which ensures that the case will be dealt with by one particular court or another in Croatia, and I haven't succeeded. You indicated that we could be confident the case would be heard by the -- a special court. Is there a legislative structure that ensures that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. This legal framework exists, yes, and it is to be found in the law on the application of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal and on prosecutions under international law, and this was enacted on the 24th of September -- October --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it refers to the cooperation of the Republic of Croatia with the ICC. However, part of these provisions are also applicable to cooperation with the ICTY. Article 49 of this law expressly provides that Article 28 is to be applied when cooperating with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. If Your Honours have at their disposal a translation of Article 28, I will not read it out aloud now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have it. I missed the significance of it as I looked, so I'm very grateful for your assistance. Thank you. And I'm sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, I will now bring my contribution to a conclusion, and of course I'm willing to discuss the details at a later stage. We have concluded our submission by saying that the key issues which will arise if this case is referred to the Republic of Croatia can be solved through cooperation and, as we have said, a creative interpretation of certain provisions of the substantive and procedural law of the Republic of Croatia. If I may, I would like to refer to a paper published by His Honour Judge Orie commenting on the Statute of the ICTY, where mention is made of the fact that judicial interpretation of the norms of statutory law is one of the key elements of its successful application. I apologise if my quotation was not verbatim, but that is how I understood it. Therefore, I would like to conclude by asking that this Chamber decide to refer the case to the Republic of Croatia, as there are no significant obstacles to such a decision. I believe that such a decision would be in line with the Security Council Resolution 1503 of 2003 regarding the completion strategy of this Tribunal, which is based on the fact that the strengthening of national jurisdictions is of crucial importance for the principle of the rule of law. I would also like to mention in passing a report from the Secretary-General from the United Nations about the rule of law and the transitional judiciaries in post-conflict societies issued by him on 23 August 2004 where among numerous conclusions a request is made, and I will quote it in English: "A request is made [in English] and Security Council's Resolutions and Mandates, point (H): Avoid the imposition of external-imposed models and mandate and fund national needs assessment and national consultation processes with the meaningful participation of government, civil society, and key national constituencies to determine the course of national justice and restoration of the rule of law." [Interpretation] Seeing this recommendation in a broad manner, we believe that the decision to refer this case to the Republic of Croatia would meet such a purpose. Thank you, Your Honours, for giving us leave to put forward our amicus curiae brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Krapac, for your intervention. I'd now like to give an opportunity to the representatives of the Government of Croatia. Professor Horvatic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an opportunity for me to greet you all, Your Honours, the representatives of the Prosecution as well, members of the Defence, and one of the two amicus curiae, friends of the court, Professor Krapac, who has been a colleague of mine for many years. It was very well stated at the beginning of this session that we're dealing with a very important issue because we are deciding for the first time on a matter of deferral, pursuant to Rule 11 bis, to another court. For me, as a man of science and as a man of practice, I find this especially dear to my heart, that is to say as a representative of the Republic of Croatia and as a representative of the country who, following a decision of this Honourable Trial Chamber, will be given this opportunity for the first time. Within my professional curriculum, this will be a red letter day. International criminal law in its development has truly been not only creatively but otherwise faced with numerous challenges, challenges of a legal understanding and interpretation of the matter in hand and political assessments as well. This particular case and the application of Rule 11 bis will bear up this observation of mine and I hope that I shall convince you of the properness of the case in hand. The second observation of the case I would like to make addressing this Tribunal is that it happens very rarely that we have before a court of law almost complete agreement on the part of the Prosecution, putting forward a request; the Defence, which agrees; and amicus curiae, who fully supports what is being proposed; and the Republic of Croatia, which welcomes it and would be happy to take it upon itself to conduct the case. So I don't think there's any conflict or dispute in this matter that the parties, the amicus curiae, and the state to which the indictment may be referred agree that that is what Rule 11 bis enables. But of course, there are a series of questions linked to this that have to be discussed because the court ruling, the decision made by the Tribunal, will not base itself on general agreement because this Trial Chamber is duty-bound and it will fulfil its duties, I will am convinced, and respect them fully, apply Rule 11 bis as it deems that it is stipulated, as is written, and that it will interpret it as the rule has been written, and this will be a first. In the reasonable demands made by the Court and in an effort to adopt the request by the Prosecution under Rule 11 bis, referral of indictment to another court in the case of Ademi/Norac, and precisely to the Republic of Croatia in this example, the Republic of Croatia is fully able and has answered all questions in two briefs, one the 20th of January and the other in November. And this makes it all the more justified -- the demands made by the Prosecution even more justified. And we express our views and standpoint by which we consider that there are no impediments or obstacles that the Trial Chamber should issue an order to refer the indictment to another court in keeping with Rule 11 bis, that is to say to refer it to the Republic of Croatia and its courts. However, the series of questions that have been raised here during this morning's meeting I should like to deal with, but I would especially like to select something that I thought was most controversial, which is the application of the possibility of command responsibility as interpreted by this Honourable Tribunal to a case to which the indictment refers and which undoubtedly is applied -- in which Croatian criminal code -- the criminal code of 1993 is applied, which does not contain the provision which was quoted earlier on from the new criminal code on express command responsibility. However, I do have the official position taken by the State Attorney of the Republic of Croatia and the State Attorney office, which discussed this question. And thereby I would like to supplement what the Prosecutor said, Mr. Scott. And allow me to quote this in English in order to avoid any possibility of insufficient understanding due to interpretation. [In English] "It has been assessed so far that difficulties could arise due to the differences in the provisions of the Statute and Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Hague Tribunal evidence in relation to the legislation of the Republic of Croatia. One of the central topics discussed at the seminars mentioned above," that was the seminars for the education of judges and prosecutors with participation of honourable members of this Tribunal and from the Prosecutors, "mentioned institution of command responsibility which institution is contained in the provision of Article 7(3) of the Statute and which institution as such is not contained in the criminal code of Republic of Croatia in the time of the commission of the crime accused in this case." And after that: "A position was reached through discussion at the seminars and of opinion of the judges of Supreme Court and the general prosecutor and other prosecutors does an institution of command responsibility concerned can nevertheless be substituted for the most part by the application of Article 28 of the criminal code from 1993, which regulates the perpetration of a criminal offence by omission. "Following this, it is the opinion of the public prosecution service that the provision mentioned of Article 28 of this criminal court with the application of the Geneva Conventions and additional Protocols could for the most part substitute the institution of command responsibility in the manner contained in Article 7(3) of The Hague Tribunal Statute." [Interpretation] Your Honours, in communications with the representative of the Prosecutor today, at one point you raised a question. You asked about the application of international law before Croatian courts of law in three ways: May, shall, or should. [In English] Let me direct that it is not possible to say "should," but I am convinced that the criminal courts in Croatia shall apply this international criminal-law standards and international criminal sources for this case and other case. [Interpretation] I'm going to switch back to Croatian now. It is the position of the Republic of Croatia in complete agreement and accord with what we had heard here today, both as presented by the Prosecution and Their Honours in their interventions and by the amicus curiae and by the Defence counsel, the key words are "creativity, a new situation, the newly arisen situation, created newly by referring an indictment to another court; great flexibility in interpreting international -- national law in the sense of bringing it closer to the general standards of international criminal law, which today is rapidly gaining in content and substance, something we couldn't have dreamed about 20 or 50 years ago -- not to go into the question of belonging to the international community, how each state belongs to the international community and the relationship of sovereignty and duties binding it to the international community, not only through ratified conventions but also through the standards of customary law but that step out from just customary law and are the rights of each state accepting them in their own interests, the principles of Jean-Jacques Rousseau, in actual fact. Or the principles of creating law and laws that we use or utilitarianism. Today we have come to a time when states quite consciously and intentionally look at their sovereignty and dovetail it with the general principles of international interests and the international community at large, not only when it comes to new forms of terrorism and organised crime, but also when it comes to trying individuals and making them accountable and holding them responsible to what happened. The Croatian judiciary knows this full well. Even when there are individuals who disagree with the fact that they have been elected as attorneys and judges, they must respect the will of the Croatian state, the Croatian constitution, and the decisions of the Croatian authorities. Rule 11 bis, to which I should like to refer once again as the basis and grounds for the ruling and decision-making of this Honourable Trial Chamber, can be interpreted restrictively or intensively -- or extensively. If it is interpreted extensively it might go too far, if it is restrictive, it might be too narrow. Today we have already mentioned should it be (F) or (G). Now, if the Trial Chamber would like to ask me any specifics, I would be happy to answer their queries, but if you're asking me as indeed the Prosecution asked itself whether and in what case -- how would you -- what would you do if witness X was proposed to testify or not, would you ask the state attorney of the state of Croatia to intervene or whether you yourselves would intervene, whether the Tribunal and Trial Chamber would intervene, what the responsibilities therein would be, then I have to say that a correct interpretation of Rule 11 bis as -- and the views already presented that paras (F) and (G) in fact give full reign and then, ad minore ad maius, we know we can act thereupon. But that, Your Honours, that’s what we're all about. We're creating something for the future and we have to see what will happen in future. And the first referred case, in this case a referral to the courts of Croatia will be a test, a pilot programme in fact, which will show us the possibilities open to us, opportunities well seized, and the President of this Tribunal, Mr. Meron, said something on the subject and he was quoted by the Prosecutor about the trust and confidence placed and what the amicus curiae said, the advantage to establishing a rule of war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Rule of law, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we shall see that Rule 11 bis was not only a possibility and an opportunity, but a very good and valid instrument by which the jurisdiction of this Tribunal is adequately expanded to other states to which the indictment is being referred and the entire case is being referred. It is -- we must strike a good balance between the extensive and the restrictive interpretation of Rule 11 bis, strike the proper balance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note the transcript is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [In English] Am I too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait a minute?

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Okay. I do believe that's not my fault. Because if I am guilty for that, I'm afraid a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not even negligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: But before the court always is something where the court said -- not only surprised but I'm afraid a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid your words will not be on record because that's exactly the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We got stuck at page 59, line 19 at this moment. The Chamber would like to be informed if the transcript is restored.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: So the Chamber would like to be informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but those are not your words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: I do not remember my last words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact -- We can restart the program, but I could read to you what at least on the record were your last words. You said, "and the first referred case, in this case, referral to the courts of Croatia will be a test, a pilot programme, in fact which will show us the possibilities open to us, opportunities well seized. And the President of this Tribunal, Mr. Meron," and that's where the transcript stops. So if you please resume from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: In English it sounds better than in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's my point. So please resume from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: So, really, intention, not the penal code issue of intention, but intention of the Croatian government and 20 criminal justice system is to prove that it is possible, it can, and it 21 should do this task if it will be delivered to the Croatian criminal justice system Thank you for this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Professor Horvatic. On our programme we have as next point, but it was scheduled after the break an intervention by the registrar. I take it that the registrar is not yet present and since we have put you on a very tight schedule, perhaps it would be better to have a break now and to perhaps take even a bit more time because you're all keeping so strictly to your time limits that we proceed in an organised way. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until a quarter to 1.00, which gives us almost 65 minutes for a lunch break. --- Luncheon recess taken at 11.52 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we resume our 11 bis hearing. On our agenda at this moment an intervention under Rule 33(B) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence by the registrar because it's not only new for all of us but also new for the registrar and it may have all kind of practical implications which we might need to be aware of. Who appears for the registrar? Is that Mr. Christian Rohde?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, with Jacqueline Geis assisting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rohde, there is circulating a short list of issues we would like to address. Has that been provided to the parties as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not aware of that at the moment, but we will stick to the list and it will be provided to the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. Well, whatever position you feel best. You're addressing us as a representative of the registry, so I would not mind if you stick to your position where the registry usually sits.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. On behalf of the registrar we would like to add a couple of practical points to today's hearing that mainly relate to small items which we feel will come up to a transfer of process, if any. However, on previous experience of working with this we have identified some points which we would like to raise and we hope they are for the benefit of the Court. The first area that I would like to refer to is the transfer of case files and confidential materials. Obviously the transfer of referral data is something that would be very crucial for smooth procedures in the referral stage, if any. That includes, for example, the responsibility of an office for transferring files, for keeping files, copies of files, for records of the Tribunal. The question is: Who in the new jurisdiction receives those files so that they can be quickly processed? Question: Also how do these files -- how are these files given to the new Defence and Prosecution teams in the referral state? How to deal with ex parte material, for example, is another issue here. As to the transcripts that have been made at this Tribunal, there's a question as to whether and how they would be transferred and accessible, particularly transcripts that are confidential, in private session; redactions that have taken place or not taken place have to be taken into account; there is a question of possibly the availability of audio recordings of the proceedings in B/C/S, I believe is the correct Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. word. That may help, actually, both parties and the Judges in the new jurisdiction. The supporting material should be thought of, perhaps the initial materials supporting an indictment. There's another question whether correspondence and other miscellaneous material could be interesting for a new jurisdiction. Again, a major issue is going to be, we believe, the proper control of access and dealing with confidential documentation, the variation or the possible variation of protective measures orders should be considered; very important obviously. And then perhaps -- that sounds administrative, but there is of course a question as to the cost of producing extra files and the cost of transferring those files. They -- there may be a large volume in a case. Much easier, though, the transfer of electronic version of files that I think could be facilitated by the Tribunal. This to the files and materials. The second item we have on our list, we propose, are witness protection issues. We propose that these issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rhode, would you mind if I interrupt you and ask you one question. Under Rule 11 bis (D)(iii), it looks as if the Prosecutor is primarily responsible, that's also how I understood the last submission by the Prosecution in which they say: We'll prepare an appropriate set of documents. Has there been any discussion between the registry and the Prosecution on who is primarily responsible whether there's any complementary task for the registry, for example, providing originals of documents that have been filed. Is there any progress made in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there have been initial discussions between the management of the registry and the Prosecutor's office in this regard. No details have been discussed yet, but certainly it would be the view of the registry that the Prosecution has to play a large role in this. Yet, as the registry is sort of the custodian of documents and materials, we would proceed in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: Thank you. I was going to say a few words on witness protection issues. They will be taken into account by the Chamber, of course. One should keep in mind the Tribunal provides certain services to witnesses, certain assistance to witnesses. Obviously relocated witnesses or witnesses earmarked for relocation, which I'm not aware whether this is the case here, but this must be taken into account we feel. Witnesses with other protective measures, not as far going as relocation, their concerns should be addressed. We suggest that with the Prosecution the Victims and Witnesses Section of the Tribunal -- of the registry would assist with these things to ensure that as much as possible the witnesses are being treated in a way that allows them to give testimony in the new jurisdiction in conditions that are proper, I would say security-wise and in other relations. A I believe tiny issue in this case would be the transfer modalities of an accused. That obviously doesn't play such a role in this case. However, we feel that one point we should make, that is it would be perhaps useful to determine an exact point when the let's say legal or custodial responsibility of the Tribunal could be transferred to another jurisdiction. That's obviously relevant for liabilities and judicial responsibilities. The third point the registrar would like to raise is essential for the accused. That would be the transition of his defence that obviously raises a basket of issues. The registrar feels that immediate assistance for accused in the new jurisdiction is essential, the question of whether the current defence teams are able to assist plays a role before a national court. If they don't, there is a question of the transfer of files to a new defence team. That should obviously go speedily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps to cut this short I think one of the questions put to the Defence and if my recollection does not betray me, then I did understand Mr. Prodanovic and Mr. Olujic would continue to represent and to defend Mr. Ademi and Mr. Norac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Olujic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. By all means. I do have the intention of completing these criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, in these circumstances, Mr. Rohde, I can imagine that in future cases, issues such as right of standing and issues such as remuneration for counsel that are being paid by the state might create problems, but in this case it is a matter that does not raise that many questions and I think that was also the position taken by the government of Croatia in its recent submission. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: Thank you for your direction, Your Honour. Perhaps one last point I would like to raise, perhaps individuals benefit from legal aid at the Tribunal, and that would be an important point. I'm going to move to two issues that may have been covered by the Chamber before. I'm going to raise them quickly. One of them is if ever the new jurisdiction would feel that the testimony and any form of staff of the ICTY, possibly from the Prosecutor's office would be required, then I would point the attention of the Chamber to the immunities of the United Nations staff according to agreements and that this immunity would have to be waived for any testimony by the Prosecutor and the Secretary-General. I assume any Rule 70 material has been addressed. I assume it has that's why I will just mention the Rule and I won't say anything on it. I would like to conclude with one point on the question as to how to address these issues. In principle of course there is the possibility of court orders; however, if there are administrative issues that the Court feels can be regulated through other matters, then obviously the registrar will be able to consider an understanding on behalf of the United Nations with Croatia on technical administrative points, for example as on liaison functions and focal points for contacts and these sort of things which are usually very, very helpful in practice. And that concludes our presentation. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rohde. As far as your observations in respect of Rule 70 materials is concerned, it's my recollection that the Prosecutor addressed the issue in the transfer of documents to the new jurisdiction and that until now at least we have heard no responses or no comments or observations in that respect. Thank you very much, Mr. Rohde. Then next on our agenda is that if the Bench would have any questions or any additional questions to either amicus or the Croatian government or the representative of the registry, they would have an opportunity to put them now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have a few questions first of all to amicus. If I may draw your attention, Mr. Krapac, to page 4 of your submission, I noticed that quite some facts appear in your submission. You're certainly aware that this Chamber has not heard any evidence in relation to this case and what actually happened. And it's not quite clear for me on what basis you introduced these facts and you may understand that we might have to ignore them if there's no clear explanation whether these are which I would not think facts, notorious facts or something like that, which would not need any evidence. But if it's just your assumption and just some thoughts about it, then it's at least clear. But if you have any other basis for the facts you introduce here, we'd like to hear if you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: May I respond immediately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, some of these assertions made, if I may call them that, or perhaps I should call them statements are actually something that the friends of the Court learned about through the mass media that were made available to them. But these are Croatian mass media. We did not really wish to rely upon the media in the belief that these were basic facts, both for the Prosecution and the Defence because we assume that the parties in these proceedings have been following the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for clarifying the source of the facts you assumed here. Another question also relating to page 4, the last few lines. You've written: "It concerns the likelihood that convictions rendered by Croatian courts in the instant case would greatly contribute to the reconciliation of affected ethnic groups." A conviction might have that effect. Would an acquittal have an oppose effect? To clarify my question: Not only your submission but in more submissions we find a high level of expectations on what a trial would bring about, where most of the expectations seem to be based on a conviction as a result of that trial, which of course is still to be considered by the domestic jurisdiction. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We proceeded from the fact that the trial, if there is a referral of the case of the Croatian authorities, that the trial due to the qualities that we already mentioned because of the regulations that were passed in the meantime will be efficient and fair. If the judgement passed on the basis of such proceedings is either a conviction or an acquittal, it has to rely on the support of the public, regardless of whether this public -- well, you referred to this ethnic category, regardless of whether it is Croat or Serb -- this public I mean. Of course one can always expect a dissatisfaction on either side, but what I do wish to say is the following: For us, the key issue is that the conduct of the proceedings and the passing of the judgement should be in line with Croatian legislation and the rules of this Tribunal, which will have to be applied in accordance with Article 28 which I already mentioned. In that case, the reaction of the public would have to be the same, regardless of whether the end result is a conviction or an acquittal. In my opinion, that is the key matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I take up the question raised by Presiding Judge and ask some more questions in relation to that. In your oral submission, Professor Krapac, you mentioned role of victims, inter alia closing arguments. And here on page 4 you said that likelihood that convictions rendered by Croatian courts would greatly contribute to the reconciliation of ethnic groups. What Judge Orie and I are concerned about is, as you put, the other side of the coin. Even if it is a result of a fair trial, if the accused are to be acquitted on the ground that international criminal law is not applied to this case and if it is the case that had they been tried in the international Tribunal, conviction might have been possible. Then the things can be worsened. If you can address that matter as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we link this up to the question that we will discuss at greater length later on, and that is the differences in the structure of command responsibility between Croatian law and the law applied by this Tribunal, if we proceed from the fact that these differences can be remedied by creatively interpreting the provisions of Croatian law, then this fear which you voiced just now is at a level of a purely abstract fear, as far as I'm concerned, which is conceivable. But, I repeat, on the basis of a fair and efficient trial or criminal proceedings, the possibility is a minimal one. If we look at this case by weighing what the Prosecution will put forth, and that will be dealt with on the basis of Croatian legislation in Croatia, by the state attorney's office, and at the end of the proceedings they will be assessed in line with the provisions of Croatian law when deciding ultimately. May I remind you once again that Croatian procedural law, which like any other continental law is based on a free assessment of pre-evaluation [as interpreted] of evidence does not allow it to be arbitrary, this evaluation. It has to be subjected to a structured process. When a Court reaches a verdict, regardless of whether it is conviction or acquittal, the Court must explain the verdict and express in great detail not only the legal views that guided it when evaluating particular matters, but it also has to set out in great detail how it evaluated and assessed every piece of evidence individually and also in relation to other evidence and how they made their ultimate conclusion, either in terms of conviction or acquittal. The process is a very transparent one. Any mistake in procedure which makes this process of evaluating evidence nontransparent, according to Croatian procedural law is considered to be a grave mistake in respect of applying the law and that results in re-trial. Judges are very cautious about this. I would say that they totally shun any possibility of the possibility of abolishing their judgements in such a situation that would lead to re-trial. When this is presented in the judgement, then it makes it possible to the higher court, that is to say the court of second instance, in this particular case it would be the Supreme Court of Croatia, then there would be a total court review, just as this Tribunal does when there is first the Trial Chamber and then the Appeals Chamber and then the entire case is reviewed and then it is established what kind of mistake was made in the evaluation of the evidence and then there is an appropriate intervention. May I say this once again: I understand your concern, your fears, but I believe that at this point in time there is -- there are sufficient provisions procedurally for redressing this or minimalising this possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, for the sake of transcript, page 69, line 20, just before disappearing, you said pre-evaluation; whether it should be free evaluation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Free evaluation, yes. I said free evaluation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krapac, on page 6 of your submission you deal with Articles 120 and following with the Fundamental Criminal Statute of Croatia. I do not find in the attachment Article 123. Would there be a possibility to provide that to the Court as well, because most of the other articles are provided? Yes. I see you're nodding, so that's not on the transcript. Then my next question would be on page 9 you explain to us that like co-perpetrators, instigators are responsible only in the limits with what they intend to bring about. And you say: "However, with respect to most serious crimes with respect to chapter 15 of the criminal code of Croatia, Croatian law departs from the otherwise adopted line between the line between perpetration and complicity. It's not entirely clear to me how Croatian law departs from that. Is there any statutory provision? Is there any case law? And how exactly does Croatian law depart from the otherwise adopted line between perpetration and complicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the first question, I don't know whether the Honourable Trial Chamber will now allow me to read Article 123, which I have here. We've left it out intentionally because its title is: "The organisation of a group and instigation to the commission of genocide and war crimes." We believe that it would not be applicable here. However, if the Court wishes, I can read this particular provision or perhaps we can have it copied and we can submit it to you in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's perhaps a very practical way and we'll find a way to have it translated. So I do understand it, you left it out because in the -- in this case it's not -- well, let's say group responsibility or what you call it joint criminal enterprise or whatever name you give it, but a kind of collective conduct which results in individual criminal responsibility for those who contributed to it. If that's it and if you just wanted to say that in this situation that Croatian law departs from that but not applicable, then we would be grateful if you would just hand over the -- provide us with the text of Article 123. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second question -- I'm not sure that I understood it fully. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have to re-read my question. I think it was about -- let me just see...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which page were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was referring to page 9 and I think Croatian law departs from the otherwise -- and I was wondering how it departs but it might even be that the clue is found in Article 123 or -- you say: "Like co-perpetrators, instigators are responsible only within the limits of what they intend to bring about; however, with respect to most serious crimes from chapter 15 FCSC, Croatian law departs from the otherwise adopted line between perpetration and complicity." You continue by saying: "As already indicated, a person in position of authority who orders another to commit a crime is treated as a perpetrator rather than as an accomplice."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The concept of co-perpetrator - co-perpetrator in English, the term is - is defined in Article 20 of the basic law of the Republic of Croatia and that law speaks of it as being more individuals, a number of individuals committing an act through being an accomplice perpetrate jointly a criminal act. And each of them is sentenced to the sentence provided for the crime in question. In Croatia, the commentators of this provision agreed that it was based -- the provision was based on the so-called theory of authority over the act, which for joint perpetration demands the subjective and the objective component. The subjective component is made up of the collective will of the co-perpetrators jointly to commit an act -- or perpetrate an act. And the second objective component is their contribution to the realisation of that act, which by virtue of its importance as such that it makes up an important part of the plan to commit the act. A co-perpetrator need not directly participate in committing the act itself, the crime itself, but he must contribute to its implementation by acting effectively during the time of its commission. Each and every perpetrator shall be held accountable and responsible with regard to his own intent. And our commentators agreed over the fact that the text of another article, Article 23, para 1, of this 1993 law allows for the possibility of co-perpetration to be held with conscious intent, advertent intent, and that it allows co-perpetration in crimes through inadvertent intent.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Rather, nonperpetration of the crime. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if more than one person takes part in an act, which your question has to do with, relates to the instigation question. And in Article 21, para 1 of the 1993 law, the provision provided as for a form of co-perpetration for a number of persons through intent to commit a crime together with others. The consequence of this with the individual in question is its decision to commit a crime -- to commit an act and the commission of that act itself. That is why in Croatian law for instigation, the instigator must have committed a criminal act and that that criminal act should be deemed a crime, an attempt at crime. And then the sentence prescribed would be a sentence for a perpetrator of an act committed. The third form of an act or third form of co-perpetration for a number of people is aiding and abetting, the aiding and abetting regulating in Article 22 of the 1993 law. And that provision defined aiding and abetting as a form of co-perpetration on the part of a number of persons with intent and therefore contributing to the commission of somebody else's criminal act. The aider and abetter is meted out the same sentence or a milder sentence than the actual perpetrator. The 1993 law provided for that aiding and abetting can be extended in different ways, intellectual ways, physical ways, or by intellectually giving guidance, instructions, trying to mask the crime that has been committed and so on and so forth or providing the means for a crime to be committed, et cetera, et cetera. For the existence -- for aiding and abetting to exist, a crime must have been committed or attempting and the perpetrator themselves need not be held criminally accountable. Aiding and abetting can also be seen to have been committed by omission. I think that in that way briefly speaking about in that abridged sentence we see reflected everything that I have been saying and how Croatian law stood in 1993 and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. how it differs from the usual construction of complicity, which is applied in the practice of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Krapac. It certainly helps in understanding your submission in this respect. May I take you to page 10 of the amicus curiae brief. Almost at the bottom you write: "Another way to induce Croatian courts to recognise indirect command responsibility is to maintain that Protocol 1 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights, incriminating that neglect failures to prevent or to punish breaches of Geneva Conventions supersedes Croatian law." I have some difficulty in finding this in Protocol 1 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, which deals with property rather than criminal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is an error in the question. It wasn't Protocol 1 -- or rather, in the writing of it. It wasn't protocol of the protection for human rights, it was Protocol 1 of the Geneva Conventions. So that was a printing mistake and I thank you for bringing that to my attention to the lapsus that took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. On page 11 you explained to us that if the failure to punish contributed to the continuation of criminal activity by the subordinates, then the superior would be liable as an accomplice, that is for aiding in this activity. May I assume that you have had access to the consolidated indictment against Mr. Norac and Mr. Ademi. May I also assume that you are aware that the crimes allegedly were committed in a relatively short period of time during the Medak Pocket operation. Would the short period of time in which both the commission of crimes and the failure to punish would be situated diminish the chance of criminal liability for the impact of the behaviour of the superior on the continuation of criminal activity which lasted only very -- very short period of time; we're talking about a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our position is this, Your Honour: We are here to propose this third approach for the solution of this question, that is to say to creatively apply the provisions of the 1993 law in a creative manner, which means that -- but I should like to emphasise that would because it is a speculative question which depends of an unknown quantity and quality of exhibits and evidence that the Prosecution has in supporting their indictment. If the Prosecution were to enable the Croatian state attorney to prove before the Court that these shortcomings can be brought into relation with the dolus eventualis on the side of the accused, then in that case their condemnation - and I'm saying -- once again this is speculative - their conviction on the basis of Article 28, para 2 would be known and certain. But as I say, this depends on the quantity and quality of the evidence available, and I am not in a position to give a definitive answer to that question here and now. So hypothetically, yes; if we have or if the Prosecution has sufficient evidence to ensure that the court trying the case is assured that it is dolus eventualis. Maybe in that short period of time, maybe two days or several hours, during the time in which the events took place described in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor Krapac, since you mention creativity, while we should welcome creativity in most of our lives, should we not deal with creativity in the field of interpretation of criminal law? To put it simply, is it not contrary to the principle of in dubio pro reo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are talking here about an interpretation of legal provisions in conformity of the doctrine of in dubio pro reo in Croatia and in some other countries as well. That principle is applied in cases when there is doubt as to the factual position and this doubt and doubt over legal matters is solved by another principle what you're going to call, and I'm sure you'll remember, in dubio mitius. Who resolving a question such as this, in our opinion, would require creatively because we are dealing with legal concepts which on the one hand are -- we are confronted with the Tribunal's practice and concepts and on the other side we have Croatian legislation and their practice. And striking a balance, the right balance there. And to strike that right balance, you will need the creatively that we talked about. So in my opinion, this Tribunal should not be afraid of applying the in dubio pro reo principle in the sense that the Croatian court in applying the in dubio pro reo concept in a given situation which stems from, let us say, a piece of evidence of a lower-level standard than the one required by Croatian standards would lead to an acquittal. So I stem from the fact that the Prosecution of this Tribunal will cooperate closely with the state attorney's office in the Republic of Croatia, and that this contact will not be unilateral at -- not a one-term contact for one case, but that it would be an ongoing process, a continuing process over a longer period of time, or rather throughout the duration of the cases tried in a first-instance court. And in such cases any shortcomings that the state attorney of the Republic of Croatia must feel with respect to the quantity or may feel with respect to the quality of the evidence provided supporting the indictment, may be made up for rapidly with a joint action, if I could put it that way, between the two Prosecution offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor, but you've been so helpful that I'm tempted to burden you with yet a further question. This concerns Article 28 of the 1993 code and subparagraph 2, which provides that a criminal act is committed by omission only if the offender abstain from performing an act which he was obligated to perform. What do you see to be the source of the obligation in Croatian domestic law of the obligations which we know as command responsibility under our Article 7(3), that is to prevent crimes by a subordinate and to punish them? Where does that obligation come to be part of the domestic law of Croatia so as to attract the operation of the subparagraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me answer that question -- or rather, in order to answer that question, I should ask Their Honours to take a look at the incriminations which we stipulated which would be applicable to that case and we listed a series of those when we wrote it -- wrote down the material elements of a crime. We provided a list of incriminations with respect to war crimes. And from these incriminations, either war crimes against the population or war crimes against the sick and wounded, against prisoners of war, et cetera, et cetera, all these stipulations, we can see there in that list that in the commission of an act we also imply the behaviour of the person perpetrating the act issuing an order for such an act to be committed violating the norms of international law. So it is from these provisions that we clearly see what is the guarantee obligation of a commander of military units to do everything in his power, everything that should be done, to prevent the commission of a crime, or rather, to react in the appropriate manner, faced with a situation like that. Now, we can discuss this at length, the guarantee obligations in Croatian law. We can discuss that. But in Croatian law as in other law systems, stem from not only the direct provisions relating to certain categories of persons such as military commanders, commanders in the police force, et cetera, et cetera; they can also be deduced from some general principles. So in the practice of the Croatian courts you will find decisions, come upon decisions whereby for omission to act as a form of perpetrating an act people are punished who through the natural course of events are responsible for the behaviours of somebody else, such as a parent, for example, is responsible for the actions and crimes of their offspring, for having prevented them from the act, although this is not provided for in the criminal law. But if a child, and I emphasise this a child, so a minor who is not criminally accountable, has committed an act and the parent failed to prevent the commission of that act or crime, they will be held responsible pursuant to Article 28, para 1. So the guarantee obligation is not expressly provided for in such a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did I understand from your answer that you saw the obligation on a commander in this situation arising from the customary international law?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does arise from customary international law, but also from the incriminations I mentioned. When you look at these incriminations, you'll always see commanders involved, too, saying: Those are order such-and-such a crime, et cetera, the commission of such-and-such a crime. In my opinion, this is a simpler and more efficient way of proceeding in order to establish responsibility in this particular case, to go through Article 28, not through international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me be clear, Professor Krapac. Those incriminations you referred to, when were they enacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Krapac, you explained to us that cumulative charging is not permitted and perhaps I take a bit of a different course. Do I understand that, for example, that you could not charge the accused with murder, a crime against humanity, and that same murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war, or in an alternative way. Is that a correct understanding of your brief? Yes. My next question would be to you, Mr. Scott. Would you consider the impossibility of charging in the consolidated indictment under Counts 2 and 3 a problem for the OTP or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, we'd have to look quite specifically at the Croatian law for that to know how much of an issue it might be in the difference of the elements of the offences and what the practical problems would be presented. The reason that we -- well, one of the reasons we do it here at the ICTY is because sometimes there's different elements between the Article 3 charge or the Article 5 charge, and therefore we want to cover both possibilities. But I can't say, frankly, in the abstract what the differences might be if Croatia were to charge it, say, under Article 50 - I'm just making this up - under Article 50 as a certain set of elements and Article 51 as a different set of elements. It may be that unlike our Statute it doesn't present itself so much as a problem. But having said all that, yes, of course there could be situations where the prosecutor would find himself -- a local prosecutor might find himself more constrained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then of course the question would be whether -- you were quite clear in your earlier submissions saying that if the indictment would not cover what is acceptable in our view -- my question is now whether this would be acceptable because there seems to be an impossibility for the local prosecutors to charge both murder as a crime against humanity and murder as a violation of the laws and customs of war. So what would that -- would you say, fine? Or would you say no, let's get the case back?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, maybe I wasn't clear. I think I understand the concern and it's a fair concern, but I was just saying under Croatian law -- let's say the Croatian prosecutor wants to charge murder and there is no issue under Croatian law which -- murder can be charged alternative ways under Croatian law, there is just one murder charge. So in that context, alternative charge wouldn't come up at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's say if you would charge as murder as a crime against humanity and you had some difficulties in proving that it was widespread and systematic, then you would have to restart all over again and to then charge the accused after an acquittal on murder as a crime against humanity as a murder as a violation of the laws and customs of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The problem I'm having, Your Honour, and I'm sorry -- I understand the conceptual concern. I don't know enough about Croatian domestic law to say how it would come up, whether that is a real scenario or not. If there is one murder -- again, sorry to repeat myself, but if there is only one murder statute in Croatia and you either charge it under that statute or you don't charge it at all, then there's no issue of an alternative charge, unlike here at the Tribunal where we have Article 3 or Article 2, Article 5 charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, we have the problem that crimes against humanity were not enacted in 1993. So to that extent. But you have a solution for that as well, by saying that that should then be taken into consideration, the widespread and systematic aspect in sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We would think it would be an aggravating factor in sentencing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Karpac, if you do not charge someone with a crime against humanity because it's nonexistent in the law applicable at that time, would you nevertheless take into consideration the widespread and systematic way of committing those crimes as aggravating? Or would you have to say, well, it's not charged, it was not punishable at the time, so therefore we have to refrain from taking that into account while sentencing? And if any of the representatives of the government would have any idea on that, they are invited to respond to the question as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission I will try to answer that question briefly, but I assume the Croatian government will have something to say in this respect, too. First of all, in response to what Mr. Scott said on behalf of the Prosecution as regards this particular matter, of key importance the page we wrote on 12: [In English]: "The indictment must include a specific description of the factual basis for the charges." [Interpretation] So if the Croatian state attorney at the very beginning of the proceedings constructs in the indictment a broad enough factual basis, then during the trial this will make it possible for the Court to rely on this indictment and take into consideration when reaching the verdict those legally valid facts which are in line with the letter of the law. It is important for the state attorney's office to start with a broader factual basis, if I can put it that way very briefly. As for the legal qualification of such an offence, that is in the exclusive domain of the court according to Croatian law. And then as we said today, the Court will decide whether this is a crime in accordance with regular criminal law, that is to say whether it is murder or killing or whether it is a war crime, a crime in respect of humanitarian law, and so on and so forth. But the important thing is to have this kind of factual basis. Because if the Court does not have a sufficient factual basis, not a single conviction, either according to regular criminal law or these special regulations that have to do with responsibility for the commission of war crimes, will not be possible. That is where we can find the set of the most important practical questions that could be raised if this case were referred to the Croatian authorities. It's not that important whether it will be qualified as a war crime against the civilian population or a war crime according to the provisions of international humanitarian law and so on, or whether it is an ordinary murder according to general criminal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Professor Horvatic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard the friend of the Court and you said that perhaps the Croatian government could say something in this respect, too. It seems to me on the basis of the debate is the problem is smaller than it may seem. I'm saying this both on the basis of what I heard from the Prosecution and from the friend of the court, namely in accordance with the position held by a Supreme Court judge which I obtained while preparing for this, there is a comparative analysis that I fully concur with, an operational analysis of crimes against humanity from the law of 1993, the Statute of this Honourable Tribunal, according to which a single conclusion can be reached. Since the protocols in the Geneva Conventions are referred to, practically the outcome is the same on both scores. It is a question of the technicality of the accusations. When reading the indictment against Ademi and Norac that was issued by the Prosecution before this Tribunal, of course Croatian Prosecutor will adjust it to Croatian needs. But I am convinced from a legal point of view that this factual material which is presented here can be part of the indictment before the Croatian courts on the basis of the 1993 law by resorting to the relevant possessions of that law, certainly those that are in chapter 15, crimes against humanity and international law. When perceiving crimes against humanity in international law and individual murders that are a result of such activity, and also the jurisprudence of Croatian courts to date has not denied the possibility of acting in accordance with dealing in an adequate manner according to the 1993 law with crimes against humanity, it is possible to have an indictment; and if what is proven is what was attempted to be proven before this court, too, there is no reason why the court in Croatia would not rule in the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor Horvatic. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might intervene for a moment. Just focusing on the discussions over the last few minutes and the question that you put to me some minutes ago, Judge Orie. I think that now that I've heard some more, if the question came up that could the Prosecutor, Croatian Prosecutor, in the same indictment, say indict the charge, both murder as a typical domestic crime and at the same time charge a violation of war crimes under Article 120, I guess that's the question and I don't know what the answer is to that or perhaps each the amici or the Croatian representative could tell us that. If that's what they would consider to be a cumulative charging, that's one question. Then I could see the scenario where the Prosecutor is going to say I'm going to charge murder and I'm going to charge war crimes against a civilian population. I'm not sure whether that would be allowed or not. The second part of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say, apart from the example I gave, where are the limits of cumulative charging, because you could say that it was -- I would say all the charges are related to a same conduct, limited area, limited time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. And the second part of that for the Chamber to consider if it wants to put these -- raise this or not. But at looking at the amici brief for submission on page 12, I'm wondering whether perhaps, and I say perhaps, not again so much differences might appear they talk about at that same paragraph where it says: "Nor are cumulative charges permitted." But it goes on several lines below that: "If proof-taking at the trial points to a different set of facts than the one described in the charging papers, the prosecutor must amend." Now, I'm not sure if that's prosecutors from a common-law system, and Judge Parker may -- I'm not sure about the practice in Australia, but conforming the indictment to the evidence, were that change to be made, right at the end of the trial -- you get to the end of the trial and say we didn't really prove murder, you proved a war crime, so we're going to amend the indictment at the end of the trial before it goes to verdict. If that was the situation, I don't see that is so different than what we do here in cumulative charging. What we say is you can cumulative charge, but once you get to conviction and sentencing, you can only have one sentence. To that extent, they may both be coming to the same point, the same conclusion by different means. You can't cumulative charge, but at the end of the case you can conform the indictment to the evidence. You should have charged this or not this. Or, at the ICTY, you charged murder under Article 3, murder under Article 2. You can't get a sentence for both so they merged essentially for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least I notice at this moment that if you amend the indictment at the very end of the proceedings, then at least the Defence might have a problem because they have defended against another indictment and have not presented any evidence which suddenly becomes relevant due to the change of the indictment at the end of the trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, and it varies -- I realise that it varies from system to system. My limited understanding that in some systems conforming the indictment, the charging document, at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the end of the evidence is not uncommon. That's as far as I can take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Parker, if you would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know that the position in Australia will help very much in the determination of this case, but it is there possible to amend the indictment at the end of the proceedings to conform with the evidence, but only within the framework of the existing charge. So that if in some detail or particular the evidence has varied, then the indictment may be amended in that respect. But one cannot substitute a different charge for that which is charged. However, we do have cumulative and alternative charging so that an indictment may well contain many, many charges, some of them cumulative, some of them alternative to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Orie, my intervention may or may not have been helpful. I was just trying to see if that could be assistance on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not going to express myself on how helpful it was now. Yes, Professor Horvatic, you would like to add something? Because this is a discussion of cumulative charging which --

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that my legal knowledge and experience once again leads me to say that I don't see a problem in the dimension of alternative and cumulative that we were presenting here, those factors. So I'll allow more experienced lawyers than myself to say that I am an ignoramus. But if I read Article 120 of the crime against the civilian population, for example, from Article 163 and it reads, you have it in English, I believe, in the catalogue of incriminations from the -- provided by the friends of the court. It says: "If anybody violates the international laws during war, occupation, et cetera, and orders an attack against civilian population, or settlement, or individual civilians or individuals incapable of combat, the result of that -- and if it resulted in death" -- then I feel that if death here is explained as well as heavily bodily harm or harm to health, et cetera, "can be a manner in which we can transcend the cumulative and the other form. But what we said with respect to the amendment of the indictment according to the practice of our law courts does not present a significant problem, because debates in their continuity have their dynamics. But those who say it would be difficult are also right, or difficult to implement, or difficult to the accept for the court if at the end of a debate or in its final stages one would appear with some new vital facts and evidence which would significantly change the indictment. But here we have a factual substrate which from the very beginning of the proceedings before a Croatian court of law or jurisdiction in the case this Trial Chamber should rule positively, would be sufficient for it to adapt to the needs and requirements of the criminal code and material laws of the state of Croatia. And the overall construction of giving way was started and lasted here this morning when we reached agreement. We agreed that there were no vital problems and essential problems in the application of law before this honourable Tribunal and what would be applied in the national courts of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krapac, you would like to add something to that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to add to that the representative of the Prosecution, Mr. Scott, noticed very well that in the sentence -- the penultimate sentence on page 12 it said that the Prosecutor must amend the indictment. I should like to remind you that in the Croatian criminal law, the basic principle and substantive law, the basic principle regulating the state attorney is the principle of the legality of criminal persecution or the principle of mandatory persecution, as it is in English. So as soon as he sees that the evidence has changed during the examination-in-chief, the indictment must be amended and added on to. Now, this brings us to the question that you raised as to how the Defence will react in a case like that, and in a case like that, the law on criminal proceedings provides that the provision that the basic proceedings be put off for as long a time is necessary for the Defence to prepare itself for the new indictment and the charges under the new indictment. And I'd also like to remind you that the basic trial and proceedings is slightly different in structure than the trial is -- than a trial is in the Anglo-Saxon process. The trial is a concentrated process and it is an event which evolves quickly from beginning to end, from the indictment via the evidence to the rulings at the end. The trial or main proceedings under Croatian law is subject to a longer period of duration with the possibility of delays along the way to settle legal questions, but even more so to amass new evidence or to react to a situation highlighted earlier on if the evidence shows that the situation was otherwise. And this brings us to the difference which at first glance seems to be great when we say that we do not have cumulative charges in our own system is not that great upon closer inspection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krapac, we are close to having heard the parties and the other participants in this hearing for another one hour and a half. I would briefly return to some very specific questions on the matter of the relationship between domestic law and international law, and I'd like to ask you or the representatives of the government about the constitutional aspects of that. The nulla pena rule, or the nullum crimen rule as it's sometimes said, is as I understand it correctly at this moment part of the constitution of Croatia. Is it correct that we find this in Article 31 of the constitution? Yes, I see you're nodding yes and I see nodding everyone yes.
