Has this provision, this constitutional provision been amended recently or has it taken its form especially in view of what I - it's not from an official source - understand it refers to, not only law but international law? Was that in this provision already in 1993? And I read to you what text of Article 31, Section 1 I have in front of me, and please correct me if I have got a wrong version. It says: "No one shall be punished for an act which before its commission was not defined as a punishable offence by law or international law; nor he may be sentenced to a penalty which was not defined by law if a less severe penalty is determined by law after commission of an act such penalty shall be imposed." First of all, is that the correct language of Article 31, Section 1, of your constitution? I see again nodding. And for the sake of the transcript I translate nodding in an affirmative answer. Then was the reference to international law in Article 31 already there in 1993? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the constitution dating to 1990 which was in force during the time that the criminal code was applied, this one, and as a constitution it had stronger force than the law. In the new law, that is to say the 1997 law which comes into force in 1998, this was literally taken over and that's why the existing law from 1993 was not changed, was not amended, but it was subject to the constitutional provision with nullum crimen sine lege was interpreted on the basis of what you read out from Article 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My next question would be about what I think might be Article 140 of the Croatian constitution, which, at least in the text I have in front of me reads: "International agreements concluded and ratified in accordance with the constitution and made public and which are in force shall be part of the internal legal order of the Republic of Croatia and shall be above law in terms of legal effects. Their provisions may be changed or appealed only under conditions and in the way specified in them or in accordance with the general rules of international law." First, is this the correct wording of Article 140 of the Croatian... Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question to you would be: Article 140 refers only to international agreements but not in whatever way to general principles of international law, neither to customary international law. Should we understand this to limit the effect of Article 140 to international agreements only?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please put your microphone on, Mr. Horvatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that a question to the amicus curiae or to the state?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's a question to whomever could answer it, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MULJACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the constitutional provision which speaks about the fact that international conventions or international agreements are above the law and that they are automatically applied precisely indicates that in cases of this kind the provisions which were prescribed in the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols and which the Republic of Croatia in continuity, when it was part of the former Yugoslavia and after its independence as of the 8th of October, 1991, pursuant to international law throughout the time was a party to those conventions and was duty-bound by international law to respect those conventions. And by that very fact this constitutional provision, that is to say the 1990 constitutional provision, speaks of the force which has a greater force than the law, and in our interpretation than the criminal law as well with the possibility of direct application. Now, the entire sense would lie in this, the meaning of it is this: In a specific concrete case through Article 28, para 2 of the criminal code of 1993 and also the application of the Geneva Conventions which were in force and which were contain international customary law codified according to the Geneva Conventions, could according to the judge -- not only could but in our opinion must be applied in this case because the law -- or rather, the system of legal provisions is the spirit of something, it expresses the spirit of something. And if these provisions express the spirit of the law and the conventions pursuant to the 1990 constitution, then they should be directly applied through the existing relevant provisions of the 1993 criminal code, which did not provide for command responsibility, as we call it, but the Croatian courts applied this command responsibility and we mentioned a case in point here, the Sakic case, and Sakic was convicted according to -- he received the greater sentence, on the basis of Article 28, para 2 of the criminal code that was in force at the time and the Geneva Conventions and their application, because Croatia was a party to the conventions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Muljacic, I'm very assisted by your submission, but can I ask whether it is consistent interpretation with the provision of Article 28, paragraph 2 of assignment of proceedings by the International Criminal Court, which says: "The proceedings in the Republic of Croatia shall be conducted with the implementation of national substantive criminal law and criminal procedure."

utterances.speaker: MR. MULJACIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] However, a Judge has to apply international conventions that were in force as well. A Judge cannot only abide by the criminal code from that year that was applicable at the time. And of course, there are tragic principle can be applied, but the constitutional provisions have to be applied and the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. And they include a strict prohibition of that and there is the provisions of the Statute of the International Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. So that is our provision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: If I may add, as I said this morning, the position of the general prosecutor of the Republic of Croatia is the same just has explained. A position was reached through discussion at the seminars, et cetera, that Article 28 of the criminal code of 1993, which regulates the perpetration of a criminal offence by omission, following this it is the opinion of the public prosecution service that the provision mentioned of Article 28 of this criminal court with the application of the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols could for the most part substitute the institution of command responsibility in the manner contained in Article 7(3). That's the official document aide memoire given by the general prosecutor of the Republic of Croatia in July 2004 and again repeated before this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We're close to -- one small question before we... The small question is: In the interpretation of Article 31 and 140 of the constitution, would the constitutional court play any role? Would that be imaginable? Would it be all in the hands of the criminal lawyers or the constitutional court be involved in the interpretation of these provisions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot say that. If such a question were to be submitted to the constitutional court, it would have to give it due attention with the intention underlying the constitution. The constitution has a proper sequence but then also a certain spirit of getting close to the application of international law as a law that supersedes national law, because Croatia by joining the international community espoused such a position, accepting international law as a law that supersedes national law when it is constrained by a national framework only. So it is hard to envisage what could happen, but I think that the constitutional court have to bear into mind everything that we have been discussing so far and it would be hard to believe that they would take a position that would be contrary to this, but it is very hard to predict what would happen, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but not from initio. That would not be an incompetence to deal with the matter by the constitutional court. Then we'll have to adjourn again. I take it after we have this break that we perhaps spend -- at least hear a bit more from the prosecutor about the apparent friction or tension between international and international customary law and domestic law. One of the issues that have not been highlighted that much at this moment is the practical application of witness protection under the new law in Croatia. Perhaps that's -- would be a matter that could have some additional attention. And finally there has been a lot of criticism on the OSCE report as covering only the last ten years, covering a past practice rather than the actual situation. I noticed that in the November 2004 report it's more actual information that is provided, which is to some extent encouraging but perhaps not in every respect. If the parties would address that matter, whether the improvement is such -- and not by saying in general terms that it's improved, but by either using statistics or using the details given in the OSCE report, that would certainly assist the Chamber. And further, we have the thematic issues 1, 2, 3, and 4, which some of them have been dealt with quite extensively already. I would like to see whether perhaps in the next round, and we'll adjourn until 3.00, whether we could conclude this hearing. We adjourn until 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume the hearing and the Chamber expects that we could finish in the next one to one and a half hours. Perhaps I first give an opportunity to the Prosecution to make some final submissions. And if you could include in those submissions how vital command responsibility, especially command responsibility in the form of not preventing, not punishing if the superior perhaps would not have known but should have had reason to know how vital that is for the Prosecution's case. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Orie. I'll try to pull together the various parts of what's been said partly -- actually, mostly what's been said in the course of the day, including by my colleagues on the other side representing the state of Croatia. As we started out this morning, it does indeed seem to the Prosecution that the more reliable basis and the more firm foundation for the application of command responsibility in a Croatian prosecution would be international law, partly for the very reasons that Judge Kwon mentioned in the last session, that is, that we're less -- a little bit less optimistic - let me put it that way - in terms of the creative application of domestic law. Yes, those things -- all those things could happen and Croatian judges might interpret their law to reach those results. But again, we think that the application of international law would provide a better foundation for these -- for such prosecutions. We did provide -- I have provided to the registry, and if that could be distributed perhaps, a copy of Article 140 of the Croatian constitution. We had had that -- we did that over the lunch-hour and then it came out over the last session in some of the questions. I think it's there, I believe. If that could be provided. It is as I believe Judge Orie has already referred to, but I didn't want to interrupt the Chamber before with the distribution of those. The handout for the benefit of counsel is also the topic -- I think it's also in the Croatian language and the English language on the bottom. As Your Honour, Judge Orie, has already indicated this is the fundamental basis for answering Your Honour's question earlier today: What is the real authority for our position. This would be the most fundamental authority, and that is that under this constitutional provision, which was in effect in 1990 prior to the conduct that would be at issue in this case, international agreements properly ratified did have the force of national law and in fact not only did they have the force of national law but were so-called above law or superior law in the Croatian national system. I've also attached to that same handout is a -- some commentary which also touches on a difference between the dualist and monist systems. And again counsel on the other side can correct me, but it appears from what research that we've been able to do that Croatia tends towards being a monistic, a so-called monistic system in which there is the direct application of international law. We believe that characterisation plus constitutional Article 140 provides a firm foundation for the application of treaty law at least, the Geneva Conventions, to Croatian prosecutions, including those provisions providing for command responsibility. In that respect -- well, let me back up for a moment. Our research indicates that the Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols, including protocol -- Additional Protocol 1 have been binding law in Croatia national law since at least as early as October 1991 as a successor state to the former Yugoslavia, which was affirmed in the Milosevic Rule 98 bis decision, and certainly no later than 22 May 1992, when its -- when Croatia's documents were lodged or deposited. So they were in effect at the time of the conduct at issue in this case. Article 86 of Additional Protocol 1, paragraph 2 provides that: "The fact that a breach of the conventions or of this protocol was committed by a subordinate does not absolve his superiors from penal or disciplinary responsibility as the case may be if they knew or had information which should have enabled them to conclude in the circumstances at the time that he was committing or was going to commit such a breach and if they did not take all feasible measures within their power to prevent or repress the breach." In a similar way Article 87, duty of commanders, section 1 provides: "The high contracting parties and the parties to the conflict shall require military commanders with respect to members of the armed forces under their command and other persons under their control to prevent and where necessary to suppress and to report the confident authority breaches of the conventions of this protocol." That might be viewed as somewhat failure to prevent. And under section 3 it also goes on to say: "The high contracting parties and parties to the conflict shall require any commander who is aware that subordinates or other persons under his control are going to commit or have committed a breach of the conventions or of this protocol to initiate such steps as are necessary to prevent such a violation of the conventions or this protocol and, where appropriate, to initiate disciplinary or penal action against violators thereof," which we suggest is essentially the failure to punish. That is the -- those are the most applicable provisions of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Additional Protocol 1, Article 86 and Article 87. Given the fact that those laws -- both of those provisions have been adopted specifically and expressly adopted by Croatia, at least by May of 1992 and given the effect of Croatian constitution Article 140, this law clearly would apply to domestic prosecutions and provides a basis for not only the Prosecution of command responsibility, but in the language in 86, paragraph 2, the -- had reason to know language, because that provision talks about "or had information which should have enabled them to conclude in the circumstances." So we believe it also addresses that particular additional feature. We would also mention then in passing the Vienna convention on the Law of Treaties 1969, Article 26 which provides: "Every treaty in force is binding on the parties to it and must be performed by them in good faith." And Article 27: "A party may not invoke the provisions of its internal law as justification for its failure to perform a treaty." So, Your Honours, again that is the fundamental basis of the treaty law or the application of the Geneva Conventions treaty law in Croatia prosecutions. Now, going beyond that of course we also then have the effect of international or customary international law as found in the Hadzihasanovic case here, that as of the time, as of the early to mid-1990s at least, command responsibility was a part of customary law. Now, it may be, and I am anticipating some of the discussion that's gone on earlier today, since Article 140 specifically talks about treaties or international agreements, it may be that there is some question about customary law. It may be that in this situation customary law doesn't really take us much further because the very Geneva Conventions themselves and those provisions have been adopted and enforced as a matter of treaty law. So in that sense, it may be that in this particular context international customary law is less important but could still be -- we don't dismiss it. It could still be another further argument, a further basis, but it seems that the direct application of the Geneva Convention as ratified and adopted by Croatia provides a foundation. Further, Your Honours, it seems to us that based on both the papers that have been filed, especially by Croatia, and the discussion today that Croatia in particular seems to support the application of Croatian law. I've heard all of Croatia's representatives this afternoon and the amici, I think, express fundamental agreement with that principle. And I think in response -- just as one example, there was a response to a question from Judge Parker in which I think the amici's answer was that: Indeed, one of the source documents or items for a duty to act was international customary law. When you look -- I think our position or that position is further reinforced when you look at the Croatian war crimes provisions themselves. In the submission that Croatia made on law, when you look at Article 120, Article 121, Article 122, Article 124 and following, all of them start out with essentially this language: "Whoever in violation of the rules of international law." So it appears that again on the face of Croatia's own statutes as in effect in 1993 there is an explicit incorporation of international law. It's Croatia's submission on page 3 - and this came out in earlier questioning between Judge Orie and counsel - the reference to the -- to the Additional Protocol 1 of the European Convention for the Protection of Human Rights, which we had understood was indeed an erroneous reference citation to Additional Protocol 1 of the Geneva Conventions, which is just exactly the reference or the discussion that we've just had. So I think without belabouring it further, Your Honour, those are the fundamental points that we would make in terms of the application of international law to -- in particular as it relates to the issue of command responsibility. I might also just mention before turning then finally to, Judge Orie, your specific question, we might -- we would also point back -- we mentioned it briefly this morning, but perhaps in light of today's discussion we would point back to the European Convention on Human Rights, Article 7(2) which again does provide for as an exception to the law against retroactivity the application of criminal law which allows for the Prosecution of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognised by civilised nations. And indeed there's some commentary on this, including some commentary by Robertson and Merills, Human Rights in Europe, which says that this Article 7(2) was included specifically for the purpose of making sure that war crimes were covered, even if not part of national law at the time. So we think that it may very well be as an additional part of the Court's consideration, the Chamber's consideration, if there's any aspect of retroactivity that still lingers around this issue, and we would suggest that there isn't, because we would suggest that it was in force in 1993, and there is not an issue of retroactivity. But if somewhere along the way the Chamber has a concern that there is some continuing issue of retroactivity, we would just point the Chamber to the European Convention on Human Rights, Article 7(2). Judge Orie, to respond to your specific question: How vital is command responsibility to a prosecution. I would have to say - I think I cannot give any other answer - that I think that it's very important. I think to prosecute these cases - we've learned from our experience at the ICTY to prosecute these cases without the possibility of a 7(3) charge, especially the higher -- the further you get away from the ground, especially in the military context, you get away from the actual actors on the ground that 7(3) provides an important part of prosecution. And I certainly would have to say, however that cuts, if you will, that command responsibility needs to be provided. And I think, as we said this morning, if it turned out that at the end of the day the Chamber was of the view that there could not be -- we could not be confident that that would be provided for, then I think it would indeed raise a serious question. Those are my answers, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Scott. May I ask one question in respect of what you just submitted to the Chamber. You said, well, customary law might not play such a role because we have no Additional Protocol 1 to the Geneva Conventions, we have the Geneva Conventions. Could you please clarify. In the consolidated indictment, the alleged crimes are situated in a context of an armed conflict, not an armed conflict of an international character. Am I wrong in understanding that Protocol 1 applies to international armed conflicts and would we therefore not have to rely extensively on the customary law rather than on Article 86 which might not directly apply to this armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that's right. And that's exactly one of the reasons I qualified my answer to say I don't think we want to completely abandon the issue of customary law because in some contexts - and particularly in this case - I think it would be important. There might be another referral case which specifically is in the context of an international armed conflict and in that context it would be less of an issue. But I agree with the Chamber for those -- if you have only an internal conflict without the international aspect, it is an additional concern and one in which you would hope to address with -- based on customary law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's keep problems for other referral cases for the future, Mr. Scott. Then I'd like to invite Defence counsel to make final submissions. Perhaps you first, Mr. Prodanovic. And may I draw to your attention that in the additional reports as attached to the last submission by the Prosecution, the representative of the OSCE expresses some concerns of accused in Croatia that fear that the pressure to convict might be such at this moment where it might have been different in the past where acquittals of Croat accused and convictions of Serb accused and even convictions in absentia would be concerned, that now it might be the opposite, that is, that Croat accused fear that the pressure is such that they -- the pressure upon the courts is such that they fear a conviction more than they did in the past. Could you please include that in your final submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And if I may add whether you could include whether you agree on the part of Defence counsel with the direct application of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it you mean counsel for the Prosecution? You said Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On the part of Defence counsel, whether Defence counsel is in agreement, could agree to the allegation that international law could apply to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question, Your Honour. Did I understand you correctly that these are my final submissions? Should I deal with all the facts now or should I just focus on the questions that you've actually put to me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are given the opportunity, having heard all the submissions that are made today, to give your final comments on it. That means that you don't have to repeat matters that are already in writing, but if you want to highlight certain matters, then you are in a position to do so. And we ask you specific attention for these two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I'm going to start with the two questions. In our submission we dealt with the question that Judge Kwon put just now, and we think that the amicus also referred to the three ways of resolving legal problems, and that includes the possibility of directly applying international law by invoking provisions of our constitution and conventions that the Republic of Croatia signed before the time the charged crimes were committed. There is no need for me to repeat what I said this morning. We believe that Croatian legislation and Croatian law - I'm talking about substantive law now - that it provides a good basis for charging the crimes according to Croatian law, both in terms of the penal code itself and also when talking about regulating command responsibility, that is to say indirect command responsibility as in Article 3, omission to punish can be dealt with within the scope of aiding and abetting a criminal after the commission of a crime. And Article 28 deals with omission, and that is one of the ways in which it can be dealt with. As for the OSCE report and the pressures that perhaps may be resent in the Croatian public and also the very own feelings of the accused who are supposed to be tried before Croat courts, I must say that, personally speaking, I don't think they'll feel any worse than they felt until now; namely, any trial and any situation when you've been charged with such grave crimes regardless of the court that you stand before causes feelings of concern and anxiety. However, the social situation in the Republic of Croatia have changed considerably, profoundly, over the past few years. Trials against the members of the Serb minority are a matter of the distant past; we can put it that way now. And they are the ones that figured most prominently before and they were certainly below the level of acceptable standards of trial. It also seems to me - and we've already said that this morning - that the OSCE presented certain facts which certainly are not incorrect. The facts that were mentioned are objectively speaking there. But I think that the time dimension should be borne in mind, namely that certain things that were unfavourable in the work of the Croatian judiciary are basically a thing of the past. The new cases that the Croatian courts are hearing now show that some headway has been made. We will not be taking too great a risk if the case were to be referred to a Croatian court, the Zagreb court to be precise, and of course justice will be done. That does not mean that we are anticipating the verdict, whether we're talking about conviction or acquittal. But we are satisfied that the proceedings will be fair and that justice will be done in a professional manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you wanted to submit, Mr. Prodanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I will have no other opportunities to speak, Your Honour, perhaps I should add two more sentences to what I've already said or would you like to ask us to make some final statements in conclusion? So this is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Whatever you would like to say, because otherwise we might end up in repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. PRODANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm not going to repeat myself and I'm not going to say many new things. But anyway, after today's hearing I'm absolutely confident that all the prerequisites are there for the referral of this case to the Republic of Croatia, both in terms of the gravity of the crime and Brigadier Ademi at the given time, that is to say, the position he held in the military hierarchy. There is a new closing strategy, completion strategy, and quite simply the Tribunal will not be able to try all the cases that are here. I also concur with the proposal made by the Prosecution and they provided arguments to that effect. In a way I understand their ambivalent position. On the one hand they have to defend the indictment and the seriousness of the charges, and on the other hand that newly established criteria have to be met. However, it seems to me that the Trial Chamber, especially after having heard the representatives of the Republic of Croatia and the amicus curiae has been assured that the Croatian judiciary is absolutely capable of dealing with this at a proper level. And the normative preconditions are there, too, namely the relevant provisions are there for carrying out the trials in Croatia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Prodanovic. Mr. Olujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. In our written submissions we have explained in detail the reasons why we believe that this case should be referred to Croatian courts for further processing. And virtually we agree regarding the basic views presented by the Prosecution. In scheduling this hearing a rather interesting legal synthesis has been achieved, and that is that on one hand we had Professor Krapac as a par excellence expert for procedural law and the government of the Republic of Croatia engaged a professor of substantive law. And all the arguments presented today can actually be reduced to the basic conclusion that this case should be referred to the Croatian courts. One of the members of the Chamber and the president of the Chamber this morning asked me a question which I will try to answer. Of course there's always some skepticism. We are lawyers; theory is wonderful, practice, too, up to a point. But there's always a certain doubt. And I think that this dilemma - and I consider it to be an academic issue - should not cause any suspicion in our views, especially if we look at the various charges and the questions put both by the Chamber -- by members of the Chamber to the Prosecution and to representatives of the Government of Croatia. And this concern was included in the question that was put. And I would like to try and answer it. Certainly, Your Honours, no one can be convicted for acts or charges which tempore criminus suspecti were not prescribed in his country. However, the criminal legislation in Croatia has taken over the punishment of all crimes envisaged by the Geneva Convention. And punishment is envisaged both for the prosecutors and for those who ordered the prohibited act. Now, the question arises as to Article 7(3), that is failure to prevent, which is not explicitly mentioned. But, Your Honours, according to logic, not only in war but in war in particular, they are part of the institute that is known as co-perpetration. A commander has the duty to prevent any criminal action by his soldiers, and by failure to prevent or to punish, he becomes a co-perpetrator according to the laws of my country. Therefore, failure to punish a crime leads to new crimes and instigation is punished equally as perpetration of crimes, especially war crimes, when many soldiers may be watching what their commander is doing. And of course this is punishable and of course this is part of the overall structure of Croatian criminal law. Of course the Chamber has also asked the Defence what our positions are regarding some conclusions from the OSCE report. As Defence counsel for Colonel Norac, I would like to point out with respect to that report that actually these are only excerpts from the report and one doesn't realise the actual context. All this is merely statistics. Therefore, without taking too much time, it is my submission that all the preconditions have been met for this criminal case, this consolidated case against Ademi and Norac should be referred to the Croatian courts. And I do not wish to be repetitious and refer to monitoring and all the other forms of control that exist for the Tribunal to take back the case, should that be necessary. Of course, I do not believe that that will be necessary. The legislative structure from 1993 is fully compatible with the crimes that my client is being charged with. Of course the actual facts and everything else will be produced during the legal proceedings regardless of whether the judgement is acquittal or conviction. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olujic. Professor Krapac, I would like to give you an opportunity also to add whatever you would like to add. And I would put one question in this respect to you: We have been provided with later reports by the OSCE in which some case law by the Croatian Supreme Court is mentioned. The case of Republic of Croatia versus Milijan Strunjas and the Republic of Croatia in what is called the Vila Vidiva [phoen] case. It appears from the way it is presented that the Supreme Court used Articles 86 and 87 of Protocol 1 of the Geneva Conventions, at least I take it that they were referring to the protocol rather than to the conventions themselves, that used it to establish an obligation to act but did not use it as a direct basis for criminal liability. If you could include that in your final observations, the Chamber would highly appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're mentioning a judgement of the Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia which is quoted in the OSCE report. I have tried -- after receiving the Prosecution's submission dated the 7th of February, I tried to find that judgement from he Supreme Court of the Republic of Croatia. They have an electronic database which became operational about a year and a half ago, if I remember well, but it is still not complete. And the judgement that you mention I'm afraid I couldn't find in the database. And I didn't have time to obtain it in paper form so that I am unable to comment on that judgement unless, perhaps, the government of the Republic of Croatia may be able to do that. But in preparing for today's hearing I came across another decision of the first instance court in Bijelovar which was later confirmed from the Republic of Croatia from 1999. And that decision was commented on later in our professional literature on criminal law. True enough, it does not relate to command responsibility for a war crime, but it does relate to a criminal offence of illegal arrest. And in this case the liability of the commander was adjusted to the provisions on non-action or omission to act. I think this is an example of how Croatian courts at the first instance and the Supreme Court implement provisions on command responsibility. This was a case in which a commander of a prison was convicted because he did not release illegally -- an illegally arrested person in November 1991 and the guards treated this person in a cruel manner. And also he was wounded when endeavouring to escape and he was convicted for failure to act. And the court came to the conclusion that the commander of the prison had the real power in that prison where this victim was detained and also at a certain point in time he did halt the mistreatment of the victim in prison that the guards had caught trying to escape, but he did not fully prevent further mistreatment and efforts -- the person was threatened. He tried a second time to escape. He was seriously wounded and sent to hospital. In the sentencing of this prison commander, the court came to the conclusion that he ignored information on the illegal conduct of the guards which was indicative of this criminal offence of illegal arrest Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and cruel treatment of the victim, and he tried to stop such behaviour as a superior in the police on the basis of his command position had the duty to prevent criminal offences by his subordinates. And as he failed to do that, the court came to the conclusion that he was liable as a perpetrator who, through failure to act, even though there were perpetrators who actually acted but they were not identified and they couldn't be prosecuted. This is an example from judicial practice that I managed to find in the short time available to me. As for the others referred to in the OSCE report, I'm afraid I cannot comment on at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any further matter you would like to address or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this some kind of closing statement on the part of the amicus?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Take your time to raise whatever you would like to raise at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have erred in the expression used, because according to the law the closing submissions is an opportunity given to the parties at the end of the proceedings to try and bring some influence to bear on the Trial Chamber to decide in their favour. For amicus curiae, that is not unnecessary because there's no need to try and persuade somebody of something that his friend is telling him. There are just two things very briefly that I should like to comment on. It is our submission, Your Honour, our opinion that the Prosecution's decision to propose the application of Rule 11 bis does not mean the introduction of any new criteria for selecting criminal prosecution of people who will be prosecuted in this court and those who will not be prosecuted at all. The Prosecution representative Mr. Scott himself said that if a decision is made to refer the case, the Prosecution will watch very closely over what is happening to the referred case and how the state prosecution in the Republic of Croatia is acting in that given case, in the instant case. Therefore, any fear that this could mean refraining from prosecution in order to achieve some kind of economy in proceedings is out of place. And I think this should be pointed out, not only for our own benefit but for the general public as well. That is the first point. The second, Your Honour, I'm still upholding the position which I tried to intimate when I quoted the opinion of Judge Orie in his comment of the Rome Statute. It is still my opinion that your decision to possibly refer the case to the Republic of Croatia in accordance with Rule 11 bis, and I shall now quote in English will represent only a general framework. [In English] "The smooth functioning of which will depend ultimately on the procedural protagonists, especially the Judges." [Interpretation] Therefore, if through this debate today we have gained some confidence towards the judges in Croatia, and especially judges in these four specialised courts which have undergone appropriate training and attended courses together with representatives of the ICTY and others, I believe that your decision, Your Honour, in this case should be an easy one after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I could ask some minor questions I omitted in the previous session. Professor Krapac, it's -- I'm sorry all the questions are pointed to you, but it may be due to the courtesy of the representative of Croatia, but I will leave them at liberty if they wish to answer to my question. Page 8 at the bottom of your -- at the first paragraph you referred to a crime of aiding a perpetrator after the crime and failure to report a crime. If you could tell us the statutory sentence or the scope of punishment possible, according to those provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Kwon, may I quote the provisions of the law from 1993, then I'm going to refer to Article 22, which reads as follows: "Whoever aids anyone in the commission of a crime shall be punished as if he committed it himself or can receive milder punishment." That means that if the court declares someone guilty of aiding and abetting, the court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor Krapac, you referred to Fundamental Criminal Statute of Croatia, Article 116 and criminal code of Croatia Article 176. If you can find those Articles, you can forward them later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I meant to do, to quote Article 120. But Article 22 that pertains to aiding is in the so-called general part of that law, whereas 120 and the other ones are in a separate part that only contain a list of crimes and the punishment envisaged. May I just add one more sentence: "A judge who finds someone guilty of aiding the commission of a crime has the power to mete out punishment which is equal to that -- mete it out to the perpetrator." That is to say, that if Article 120 envisages a minimum sentence of five years imprisonment, up to 20 years imprisonment as a maximum sentence, then he can punish him with any sentence within that scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're not following my question. Do you have your report with you? Amicus report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could draw your attention to page 8 of your report. The last line of first paragraph in English page you say: "Article 116 of FCSC and Article 176 of CAC."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. I focused on the basic question of aiding and abetting and the possibility of punishing an aider and abetter if a causal relationship can be established in terms of the commission of the principal crime, whereas you have referred to a different case when this is not possible. In such a case, then the conduct of that behaviour falls under a different part of the criminal law. That is Article 116 that you referred to just now. If you do not have the Article in question here, I can read it out. But if you believe that is not necessary, we can provide actual copies subsequently. May I just mention that according to Article 116, the punishment envisaged is between one and ten years' imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is related to the limit to the duration of preliminary detention. I wonder, the meaning preliminary has the same meaning of pre-trial, whether that -- am I correct in so understanding? Does that limit also apply to the trial period or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. According to the provisions of the current law there are time limits in terms of what you call preliminary detention until a verdict is passed. Therefore, these time limits of preliminary detention are actually calculated twice. In the preliminary proceedings, in the pre-trial proceedings, there is one particular limit; and then from the moment when the trial begins and until the very end, until the passing of the verdict, there is a different amount of time that may be spent in preliminary -- in detention. We thought that in the preliminary proceedings before the actual trial begins, the time spent in preliminary detention could be calculated according to the special law on preventing corruption and criminal behaviour. That had to do with the preliminary procedure involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me be clear: Do you have to finish the trial in a year's time from the date of his arrest?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question is: Could you turn to page 17 of your report, or rather, from the bottom of page 16, which is a part of your summary of argument. There you said: "Nevertheless there would be no problem under the existing Croatian law to convict a commander for failure to prevent a crime, provided that he knew that the crime was in preparation." And then you go on to say: "And even if he did not know that the crime of his subordinates was foreseeable he could still be liable on the basis of a type of culpability that shades into advertent form of negligence." Is it a fair description or summary of what is stated in the main text?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAPAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the answer is yes because we tried in two or three sentences to actually summarise what we wrote about what mens rea is about as far as command responsibility is concerned. May I just add one more point. A key question that will be raised here is the question of evidence. Will the Prosecution or the state attorney's office in Croatia have proper evidence in their hands which will be conducive to this possibility of establishing that a commander knew of crimes that were being prepared and committed, or even if he did not know, could he have known about that, or rather could he have foreseen that these crimes could have been committed. If the Prosecution has evidence to that effect, the court will not have any obstacles in the path of reaching such a verdict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Krapac, I'm a bit ashamed of myself. You have drawn the attention two times to a quote of myself. I think the parties are entitled to know the context, so if you could provide them the context in which I wrote or said that, and this would certainly help me to find it for myself as well, because it's not clear in my recollection anymore. But I take it that the quote is correct. Then I'd now finally like to ask the representatives of the Government of Croatia to address this Chamber. Professor Horvatic, I would invite you also to perhaps pay a little bit more attention to the phrase you used twice when you were referring to a statement or a document not known to me but two times you used the phrase that for the most part the problems covered by Croatian law. Of course my concern is: What happened with that part which is not -- which does not belong to that most part. And I earlier invited you to give us further information to extend possible on the statistics on the performance of Croatian courts in view of the criticism expressed before by the OSCE, because if taken knowledge of your general approach but if there's any more detailed material. And I also invited you before the break to give us some more information on the practical application of the legislation which has been adopted in view of witness protection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your questions, Your Honour. First of all, talking about statistics I personally and as a representative of the government believe that statistical data are sometimes such that even when we expect them to provide an answer they are very unreliable bases for such an answer. Insight into each and every case was for me the basic source of knowledge. I'm resolutely against statistical data regarding the number of acquittals or convictions being used for any kind of judgement about any kind on this globe. Only insight into the file and the final judgement of the court. Is it possible to scientifically comment on the application of the law? And when certain reports, such as those mentioned here, refer to first-instance judgements which the second-instance court in the Republic of Croatia, that is the Supreme Court, reversed or rescinded, then my understanding was not that this was criticism of the conduct of the first-instance court, but rather an expression of the way in which the judicial system in Croatia is functioning and that the final decision rests with the Supreme Court. The number of cases processed before Croatian courts could be divided, as we heard this morning and the afternoon, into two time periods. The second period that covers the last two or three years, it is difficult to be more precise in terms of days and months, but this is a period of a definitely different approach resulting from education, realisation, and the approach of Croatia to meeting the higher standards of the rule of law. And when that even a young country, if counted from the moment when it became independent, has shown to have matured in all respects of state powers, executive, legislative, and judicial in particular. As regards witness protection, I take the liberty of drawing attention to our report. The second from January this year and on page 15 under the heading, I'm quoting the law: "The Witness Protection Act of October the 1st, 2003, People's Gazette, 163 -- [In English] And all articles contained. I must say, and I'm fully convinced that this act is not only in accordance with similar acts in other countries, but it is also in accordance with the spirit and the behaviour and the sources in this court. So this Witness Protection Act --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Horvatic, perhaps I have not been clear enough in my question. The law is quite clear. It's -- in full detail it has been presented as an annex with all the different temporary measures or final measures, relocation, everything's there. But the question was mainly, and I could have put that question to Professor Krapac as well because he also did not elaborate that much on the application of that law, the -- is it already used in practice, what are the results? That's what I was mainly interested to hear about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I can say that in the Ministry of Interior and the Ministry of Justice, a special service has been set up to implement this law. We have had several cases in connection with organised crime. We had several cases connected to war crimes, and I'm quite confident that only now if the case is referred and if the need arises for witness protection, only then will the implementation of that law come fully into practice. The state of Croatia guarantees that that law will be implemented organisationally and in actual fact. It is in our interest, as opposed to some other laws which may be of lesser significance, and we have certain difficulties in implementing them of an organisational and financial nature, this law certainly has priority. Allow me to use this opportunity to respond to some questions from the secretariat if I may, from the registry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. May I understand that where the Prosecution on page 5 of the January [sic] submissions said that this legislation is not well tested yet, that that's to some extent true. And that as a matter of fact this first referral case might be the test case for the application of this Witness Protection Act? Because you were rather vague in your answers that by saying in some organised crime cases and in some war crime cases -- I mean, the system works upon an application to be decided by this committee. How many applications have been made in war crime cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In war crimes, to the best of my recollection, there were two requests and they were withdrawn because those witnesses did not appear at all. That is as far as I can remember about war crimes. But the service for witness protection that has been established, including identity protection, this service in the Ministry of Internal Affairs and the Ministry of Justice is there on a stand-by basis should such a request be made indeed in this referral case or in any other. That is why I'm saying that the Croatian state guarantees that the law will be implemented. We don't have enough experience to be able to give you the number of cases that we have had to apply this law. We had three cases in crime prevention when this law was applied, but all the services are in place and it is quite clear what needs to be done at a given moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the question by the registry about the transfer of the file and the material, an answer has partially been given because Rule 11 bis provides for this and you quite correctly said that the Prosecution is duty-bound to provide the court with all the necessary material and especially supporting material with the indictment. As to whom this material will be given and in what way, our answer at this moment would be primarily to the public prosecutor, to the state prosecutor in Croatia. We're a bit skeptical with respect to any delivery of material electronically because this can cause certain problems which we are already encountering and which have been informed about by Defence teams in this Tribunal. There's so much material so that delivery and copying and selection of that material can be of course of difficulty. So I would suggest that the Prosecution and our prosecutor's office could easily come to an arrangement through a liaison officer as to how this should be done. And finally, the question of testimony by persons enjoying immunity. This may not be acceptable for the Court if I say: If that should occur then the instruments legally available will be resorted to. But I believe that the Croatian judicial system, as it has done in relation to persons with diplomatic immunity which could have testified in other cases that are not related to these were very cautious and preferred to give up that witness than place him in a position which could deprive him of diplomatic immunity. So I think the matter will be discussed, should it arise. And finally, fully agreeing with what Professor Krapac as an amicus has said, I as a representative of the government also should not have any closing argument to offer. But at the end of this very tiring day for you and for us, I would like to say that in this courtroom, regardless of the outcome and your decision, which I hope will be a positive one and will be in favour of the Prosecution, in doing so we would be taking a step forward in the development of international criminal law. And I assure all those with any interest in the matter and above all this Trial Chamber, that the Republic of Croatia is -- will accept and take over the indictment and the case with the highest possible responsibility. We're obliged to do this for many reasons, but one which I consider to be of the greatest importance is the one listed under (F) of Rule 11 bis, and that is: "At any time after an order has been issued pursuant to this rule and before the national court acquits or convicts the accused, the Trial Chamber may at the request of the Prosecutor, and upon having given to the state authorities concerned upon it opportunity to be heard, revoke," that is the point, revoke the order and make a formal request for referral under the terms of Rule 10. If this were to happen, and the Croatian government and its judiciary will do everything it can to avoid it, then this would send a very bad message for The Hague Tribunal, which we respect, and for the Croatian judiciary. That is why very seriously and with full responsibility we shall participate in this undertaking which has been embarked upon and when cases will be distributed to other courts as well, I hope will be successfully completed to the benefit of mankind, helping to avoid the horrors committed through war crimes and crimes against humanity. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Horvatic. May I ask for one clarification. You said in relation to immunity and in response to one of the observations made by the representative of the registry, you said: "The question of testimony by persons enjoying immunity, this may not be acceptable for the Court if I say if that should occur then the instruments legally available will be resorted to." I did not fully understand what court you were specifically referring to, whether it was this court or the -- one of Croatian court and what instruments legally available you were referring to. If you could please explain that in order to avoid whatever misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HORVATIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A representative of the registry of this Tribunal, among the questions and problems highlighted in connection with referral mentioned testimony of certain persons with immunity from this Tribunal should they be called to testify in a Croatian court in connection with the referred case. And my response was that as for the two, when certain persons that do enjoy immunity in other cases, but not war crime or crimes against humanity, may be in some very low-level slander or something like that, every effort was made to avoid questioning people with immunity. So I believe that they will not insist on such persons testifying unless it is of absolute crucial importance to establish the guilt or innocent. So no request would be made to remove immunity from persons who may be called to testify. But I also added that one cannot foresee things but that one would always act, that we would act in accordance with the rules. So this is something that never really occurred to me, but as the representative of the registry mentioned it, I felt it my duty to comment on it. There were some other administrative questions such as liaison officers, et cetera, I think that this all can be resolved very simply through contact with the Ministry of Justice and the state attorney. And I think that we have experience with cooperation of this kind hitherto as well. Our own attorneys have provided assistance to the Prosecution. And after a telephone call or an e-mail, these things can function easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to say a few words about that because there might be some misunderstanding. And if, Mr. Rohde, I have misunderstood your comments, please tell me. I understand it is a general UN policy which is written down in instruments that UN employees for reasons of their safety and apart from that also for reasons to not -- not to be obstructed in performing their duties in the future, that the UN requires whatever court before calling a UN employee as a witness to request that immunity will be lifted. It is the experience at this Tribunal that if you keep a close eye on the interests involved, that the United Nations usually has an open eye for the needs of court to hear testimony of witnesses. So it's the experience in this court at least that usually an agreement can be reached so that the court will have available the necessary information for making its determinations and, at the same time, that the interests of the UN and the safety of UN employees is sufficiently guaranteed. Mr. Rohde, if I misunderstand the position, then please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for the statement. No, you interpreted this correctly. The only point that was important for us that Croatia recognises the immunity but of course is aware of the possibilities to waive such immunities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Rohde. I take it that everything has been said, asked, and answered what we thought that would need to be said, need to be asked, and need to be answered. Since I see no nodding "no," I'd like to conclude this hearing. We have paid attention to those requirements under Rule 11 bis of this Tribunal, especially gravity and the level of responsibility. We have not even touched upon others which are, I would say, self-explanatory, which do not need any attention. We have also paid broader attention to the question of whether the applicable substantive law of Croatia, if the case would be referred, whether that substantive law would cover the type of conduct and the type of responsibility for which the accused were charged before this Tribunal. We have spent ample time on the procedure, the criminal procedure in Croatia, both on the abstract level and on the concrete level, and have addressed the question whether it has reached or is at a level which would allow the Tribunal to refer cases or at least this case with full confidence. We've also raised issues in respect of the relation between this institution, the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, and the Croatia courts once the case would be referred, but as long as no final judgement has been delivered. The Chamber is grateful for the parties in assisting the Chamber in preparing a decision. The Chamber is also grateful for the representatives of the Government of Croatia, Professor Horvatic, Mr. Muljacic, and Mr. Milevoj, to have informed the Chamber and to have answered all the questions we have put to you. And finally, the Chamber would like to thank Professor Krapac for acting as an amicus, and through his observations he made perfectly clear that he fully understands what it means to be a friend of the court, that is no closing argument but finally in the final submissions to draw the attention to those matters a friend should know. We invite you, Professor Krapac, to also thank Professor Damaska for having contributed and having participated in the preparation of the amicus curiae brief. Finally, I'd like to draw the attention of the parties but also of the Croatian government and the amici curiae that Rule 11 bis has been amended on the 11th of February. The amendment has been published on the 15th of February and enters into force - so it's not in force yet - on the 22nd of February. It's just for your information that I draw your attention to that. The Chamber will consider the matter. The Chamber will see whether it will deliver a decision right away or whether it needs further information in due course. You will either receive a decision or you will be addressed in another way if the Chamber thinks that a final decision cannot yet be made at this moment. We stand adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.28 p.m.
